title: A Harmless Act of Halloween Rebellion
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
Last Halloween, I answered a knock on the door to find a young trick-or-treater dressed as a toilet
Not just any toilet— Skibidi Toilet , a disembodied head that pops out of a toilet and is a villain of the eponymous YouTube miniseries about an army of such creatures conquering Earth
I was visibly puzzled and asked him a series of questions
Was Skibidi his first name and Toilet his surname? Was he a man stuck in a toilet, or a new, hybrid organism? He looked at his friends and laughed; I smiled awkwardly as I distributed Airheads
When I was a kid, Halloween featured a reliably recognizable cast: Darth Vaders, Little Mermaids, and plenty of Spidermen
But the internet’s memes have inevitably bled into costumes

For every zombie, there is now also a John Pork (an anthropomorphic pig in a red flannel that keeps calling your phone), a Ballerina Cappuccina (a cappuccino that performs ballet in a pink tutu), and a Tung Tung Tung Sahur . (Sahur is an AI-generated bipedal kentongan drum with a human face that wields a baseball bat
He’s also Italian .) Wearing a costume that successfully confounds grown-ups could be considered a harmless act of Halloween rebellion on a day known for mischief
This holiday has long marked an occasion for kids to assert an us-versus-them mentality toward adults

In 2012, Emily Chertoff compiled a history of the Halloween pranks for The Atlantic , recounting how the antics once got so out of control that in 1923, Omaha’s “police commissioner came up with a solution: he would recruit 500 of the city’s ‘worst boys’ to serve as ‘special policemen’ on Halloween, turning over to each a badge and a beat.” Soon enough, “every boy in the city” wanted to qualify, according to an anonymous author in The New York Times
For decades, cities introduced creative solutions to quell the discord on All Hallows’ Eve
In 1938, “Boston’s police commissioner gave ‘engraved awards’ to ‘the three schools in districts which showed the “least vandalism” on Halloween,’” Chertoff noted
She explained that after World War II, trick-or-treating took off as one of the most successful interventions to actually stem Halloween’s mayhem

It also led many people to lament the death of the holiday. “The children who come to my door will remember All Hallows’ Eve as a night when they sold their right to rebellion for some sugar in expensive wrappings,” Lois Phillips Hudson wrote in this magazine in 1962
The rebellious spirit of Halloween wasn’t gone, though
Costumes were another battleground between kids and grown-ups, and the freedom to express oneself was at the center of this clash. “On Halloween a boy can’t wear anything feminine
The idea of lipstick horrifies a father,” Evelyn Goodenough Pitcher quoted one mother saying in The Atlantic ’s March 1963 issue
The generational divide has taken on a new form in today’s algorithm-inflected celebration

In 2024, Kate Lindsay argued against such niche costumes . “The meme invasion threatens the spirit of Halloween,” she wrote in The Atlantic . “The costumes aren’t intended for my—or any other partygoer’s—consumption

They’re for our phones.” Indeed, at a Halloween party I attended in Bushwick, I bumped into someone dressed as the grandfather who ate paint thinking it was yogurt (a real person whose image became a meme )
Last year, photos went viral of adults donning “six-seven” outfits at Halloween, sounding the death knell for the meme
Children, though, aren’t always performing for the algorithm
Maybe their real Halloween joy comes from laughing at a perplexed adult holding a candy bowl on their porch
Although pranks have faded from Halloween’s traditions—the “trick” has surrendered to the “treat”—little rebellions remain

The mischief-makers of the early 20th century might have been pleased to see legions of giggling Tung Tung Tung Sahurs roaming the streets, while mystified parents ask one another: What’s your kid dressed as?

title: Democrats Are Ready to Run Hegseth ‘Out of Town’
excerpt: M any Democrats have a post-midterm dream that goes something like this: Pete Hegseth, the push-up-loving, beardo-mocking former Fox News host who has led the P
body: M any Democrats have a post-midterm dream that goes something like this: Pete Hegseth, the push-up-loving, beardo-mocking former Fox News host who has led the Pentagon for almost two years with bombast and theatrics, is either fired or hauled before their new majority in the House to face impeachment—which would make him just the third Cabinet secretary in history to face such a sanction. “One of the first things we’re going to do in the majority, we’re going to run Pete Hegseth out of town,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to be speaker of the House should the Democrats win that chamber, declared at a rally this month, the closest he’s come to saying the I-word
Hegseth helped steer the U.S. into war with Iran, and then failed to deliver victory
He initiated strikes against speedboats allegedly carrying narco-traffickers off the coasts of South and Central America that many Democrats view as extrajudicial killings
He pushed out scores of seasoned generals , many of whom were held in high esteem on Capitol Hill
All the while, he has flouted any notion of congressional oversight
His acidly partisan approach to Hill relations dates back to his contentious 2025 confirmation process, when he broke tradition by declining courtesy calls with most Democratic senators
And he has, in his political opponents’ view, brought a macho crassness to the job, railing against “fatties,” “weirdos,” and “beardos” and introducing hormone supplements to ensure “high T” troops

Former President Obama last weekend mocked the well-coiffed Hegseth for focusing on “the jawlines and testosterone levels of our troops” and for being consumed by vanity. “How much time,” Obama asked, “do you think this defense secretary spends looking at himself in the mirror in the morning?” From a Democratic standpoint, what’s not to impeach? Yet precisely because Hegseth and his behavior present such a ripe target for House Democrats, they might ultimately decide against pursuing that measure

After all, even if a Democratic-controlled House voted to impeach Hegseth, and even if the Democrats win a majority in the Senate and convene a trial, Hegseth almost certainly would retain enough support in the upper chamber to fall short of the required 67 votes for conviction

The alternative is for Democrats to try to rein in Hegseth without the spectacle of impeachment, relying instead on the aggressive pursuit of their more traditional oversight mechanisms—hearings, investigations, and conditions attached to the annual defense budget
If Democrats are going to go to war, as it were, with the self-styled secretary of war, they may prefer to fight a battle they think they can actually win
I f Thomas Massie has his way , Hegseth’s impeachment wouldn’t wait until the new Congress convenes in January

The outgoing Republican representative from Kentucky has said he plans to bring the articles of impeachment he filed this fall against Hegseth up for a vote during the House’s lame-duck postelection session

His eight draft articles include accusations that Hegseth plotted to conduct an illegal war in Iran (a conflict for which President Trump never sought congressional authorization) and that he approved the “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader,” a reference to the January seizure of the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro
Massie told Puck he thinks other Republicans who are poised to leave Congress may rally behind him

The vote to proceed with impeachment and the impeachment itself require a simple majority in the House. [ Read: Here’s who Democrats want to impeach next ] Democrats would likely welcome Massie’s move, even if it did no more than force Speaker Mike Johnson and Trump to come to Hegseth’s defense
A recent Politico poll showed that 63 percent of Democratic midterm voters would support impeaching the defense secretary. (Only Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F
Kennedy Jr. was a more popular target for impeachment, with 65 percent support.) And, should Massie’s effort fail, the Democrats have their own draft articles at hand
Representative Yassamin Ansari of Arizona filed impeachment articles against Hegseth in April

Her draft articles are similar to Massie’s but also include accusations of obstructing congressional oversight and mishandling classified information (in March 2025, Hegseth shared sensitive war plans in a Signal group that included The Atlantic ’s editor in chief)

Her effort has 16 co-sponsors, all of them Democrats, but she sees the ground shifting and holds out hope that Trump will get rid of his defense secretary before Congress has the chance to act. “The calls against Hegseth’s leadership have increased dramatically on both sides of the aisle,” Ansari told us. “We are really strongly pushing the president to replace Hegseth.” The White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told us in a statement that Trump strongly supports Hegseth. “Secretary Hegseth is doing a great job leading the Pentagon,” she said

Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson called Hegseth a “transformative leader” who has “slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way.” The House has impeached only two Cabinet secretaries: William Belknap, the secretary of war, in 1876; and Alejandro Mayorkas, the secretary of homeland security, in 2024. (In both cases, the Senate did not convict.) Representative Jason Crow of Colorado, a Democrat and former Army Ranger, was one of the seven impeachment managers during Trump’s first impeachment trial in the Senate, in 2020
He told us the party needed to be cautious in considering a third presidential impeachment

But he is far less squeamish about trying to remove Hegseth. “Pete Hegseth and the corruption he’s brought to the Department of Defense is at the top of my list,” Crow said. [ Read: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth ] Representative Adam Smith, who would lead the House Armed Services Committee should Democrats take over, told us that he and his colleagues will have limited powers even in the majority, especially if the administration rebuffs congressional requests for documents or witnesses
The Justice Department, for instance, under Trump’s onetime personal attorney Todd Blanche, may decline to enforce congressional subpoenas

That would make even lawmakers like Smith, typically more inclined to dig into the arcana of acquisition reform than stage a made-for-TV trial, more likely to consider the toughest sanction. “Do we try to work in a reasonable place or do we go right for the jugular here?” Smith said, referring to Jeffries’s desire to see Hegseth removed from office. “Personally I think there’s no reason to expect that Trump and Hegseth are going to cooperate with us in any way
So I think that Hakeem may well be right.” The decision could amount to an early test of Jeffries and his ability to corral the different factions in the Democratic caucus

Even as he has talked lately about running Hegseth out of town, Jeffries hasn’t explicitly endorsed an impeachment strategy. “Pete Hegseth needs to be pushed aside by the president,” he told MS NOW this week, “or we’re going to have to deal with the situation if he is not.” G OP grumbling about Hegseth’s performance has intensified over the past year

Representative Mike Rogers and Senator Roger Wicker, the chairs of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, respectively, have objected to administration plans to cut the U.S. military presence in Europe and to Pentagon delays in providing aid to Ukraine
Senator Susan Collins and others complained when Hegseth fired respected military leaders, including Generals Randy George and Chris “C

Mike Johnson panned Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution by firing squad. (Trump ultimately quashed the livestream.) Outgoing Senator Thom Tillis has described his vote to confirm Hegseth as the “biggest regret” of his career

Still, even those Republicans unimpressed with Hegseth have been loath to cross the president, and they continue to support most of Hegseth’s plans, including a boost in defense spending to $1.5 trillion. [ Read: How Pete Hegseth’s plan for a reality-TV execution imploded ] That suggests an uphill push for a conviction in the Senate—and a trial would provide Hegseth with a prominent, televised perch from which he could lambast the effort, secure in the knowledge that his prospects of conviction are remote
That may be all the more desirable for him as Trump enters his lame-duck years and the MAGA faithful search for a worthy successor
The spectacle of Hegseth in a congressional hearing room defending his troops and hitting back against Democrats could boost the presidential ambitions he is said to harbor
Trump’s two impeachments ultimately helped his political standing by giving him a clear foe; Republicans might welcome a similar dynamic with the secretary of defense in the dock
Should Democrats decide against impeachment proceedings, they are likely instead to resort to more common oversight measures
Riders to the defense-spending legislation could compel the Pentagon to comply with congressional mandates barring troop drawdowns around the world
Special Operations Command, will likely face questions over a September 2, 2025, air strike that killed two men clinging to maritime wreckage in the Caribbean
Democratic lawmakers also want to declassify the Office of Legal Counsel memo that lays out a legal rationale for those operations, and potentially bring in military lawyers to testify

Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. military operations in the Middle East, could be asked about casualties from the Iran war —those of American troops and Iranian civilians—and damage to U.S. bases in the region

title: The Rise of the Sexy-Cozy Autumn Read
excerpt: Unto every season is given a certain kind of book
body: Unto every season is given a certain kind of book
When the new year beckons a new you, self-help thrives
Cookbook recommendations abound in the lead-up to Thanksgiving
Curiously, publishers told me, Easter is big for picture books (which are easy to stick in a basket next to the chocolate bunny)
Time to bust out some Shirley Jackson (or perhaps some Stephen King or Edgar Allan Poe)
Yet the days of decorative gourds and darkening evenings have also become a boom season for romance novels—not just any romance novels, but ones targeted at both Halloween and fall more broadly
These books exist on a spectrum of snuggly to spooky: on one end, crispy foliage and adorable bookshops; on the other, the growing subgenre of horror romance
In the middle lie Halloweeny but still-sweet stories of witches brewing love potions, grim reapers falling for guardian angels, and regular old humans getting entangled with creatures of all kinds
This trend results from a brew of ingredients that include market forces, social-media trends, and readers yearning to escape the real world for a cozier one with more regular seasons
Autumnal romances are not an entirely new phenomenon, but they have really taken off in the past two to five years

Winter-holiday-themed romances used to be published around the end of September, according to Leah Hultenschmidt, the publisher of Hachette Book Group’s romance-focused Forever imprint. “People talk about the Christmas creep
But we were really creeping it,” she told me

Now, she said, holiday books are being pushed back because “fall has become its own selling season.” [ Read: The publishing industry’s most swoon-worthy genre ] Taylor Capizola, the general manager of the romance bookstore The Ripped Bodice in Los Angeles, told me that The Ex Hex by Erin Stirling was the first “overtly autumnal, overtly Halloweeny” book she noticed catching on
That book—about a witch who curses her ex-boyfriend—came out in 2021
That same year, Jeannie Chin released the small-town romance novel The Inn on Sweetbriar Lane
It’s set in fall, and features a pumpkin festival

But Chin told me that at the time, she wasn’t thinking of it as a seasonal romance, and her publisher wasn’t really planning to market it that way. ( The cover , with its pink flowers, actually looks pretty spring-y.) “As it came out, I think, is sort of when this ‘fall is the new Christmas’ thing started,” she said. “So we sort of pivoted with the marketing a little bit to take advantage of the fact that it absolutely is a fall book.” Interest has escalated since then

Whereas in the early part of this decade, Capizola might have seen five or so Halloweeny books come into the shop in the fall, by last year The Ripped Bodice was unpacking “boxes and boxes and boxes,” she said. “Just a massive amount.” One of the fall-themed novels that came out this year was Chin’s
With The Cozy Nook Bookshop , “the idea of putting that fall cozy piece front and center was there from the beginning,” Chin said

The leaves, the chill, the steamy beverages, and the beckoning of the fireplace all set the mood for what many hopeful singles call “cuffing season.” The beloved rom-com You’ve Got Mail famously takes place in fall, with Tom Hanks rhapsodizing about “a bouquet of newly sharpened pencils”—a quote that makes the rounds on social media every autumn
But there’s romance set in the fall, and then there’s fall romance. “We are giving them something seasonal on purpose,” Hultenschmidt said of her publishing imprint
And seasonal romances can be very on the nose
Take Emily Henry’s 2020 romance, a beach read titled Beach Read , that is set at a lakeside beach town and stars an author who writes beach reads
Cindy Hwang, the editorial director at Berkley, which publishes Henry, told me she thinks that the popularity of Beach Read helped launch the trend of highly literal seasonal romances
Some of these fall books practically grab you by the collar, shove a pointy hat on your head, and pour a pumpkin-spice latte down your throat
For instance, last September, Amazon published a collection of short stories for Kindle and audiobook called Scared Sexy , one of which is about a sexy sleep-paralysis demon
All of the stories feature creatures, and most mention Halloween in some way
A couple of these stories were among Kindle’s most-purchased romance books of 2025, according to the blog Romancing the Data , which tracks romance best sellers
For the same reason someone might watch scary movies or carve a pumpkin, they pick up sexy Halloween books to get into the spirit of the season
But why is seasonality something readers are particularly craving now ? It may partly follow from the rise of “spooky season” as a concept
The phrase doesn’t seem to have been used much before 2018 or so, according to Google Trends
It’s invoked as a way of extending the playfully scary energy of Halloween throughout the fall, and giving adults an excuse to partake in seasonal delights along with kids
Hultenschmidt suggested that the whole snuggly-to-spooky spectrum could be explained by the sense of uncertainty and instability pervading the culture right now
In the face of economic anxiety and political tension, people may seek safety in the comfort of a romance novel and its guaranteed happily-ever-after
Or “they want the terror of a horror novel to be like ‘Oh, well thank God it’s not this bad,’” she said

This might also explain the appeal of hybrid horror-romance books like this year’s Kiss Slay Replay by Rachel Harrison, about a woman trapped in a time loop at her best friend’s wedding, with a masked killer on the rampage and a handsome wedding guest to help her fight back. [ Read: The dark reality behind ‘cozy mysteries’ ] I also wonder if some of the appeal is a result of climate change
Seasons other than summer are getting shorter , and all seasons are becoming more unpredictable
When I spoke with Hwang earlier this month, the high in our respective East Coast cities (D.C. and New York) was nearly 80 degrees
If I wanted to catch that classic fall feeling in mid-October this year, I would’ve been better served by cracking open a book than by going outside
In addition to the comfort and the spookiness, all of the attention on fall stems from one more thing: marketing

title: The Variety Bag Has Ruined Halloween
excerpt: Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home
body: Nothing stands out, apart from the quantity of candy dumped out on the floor back home
Every house seems to buy a variety bag of seemingly random candy, and consequently every stop metes out a little more of the same treats as the previous one did or the next one will
A harvesttime holiday that evolved from traditional reflections on death is now merely another household chore to carry out on the way to mortal life’s certain end

In my memory, the trick-or-treating procedure used to go down like this: An older lady or stern man made some idle chatter about costumes and then dispensed one or three candies into my bag directly from their basket
The candy provided was particular and intentional: You got a Hershey’s Special Dark mini and a wee Mr
Goodbar, perhaps, or a few Smarties cylinders, or, alas, a handful of Bit-O-Honeys

Children identified houses by what they dispensed: Don’t miss the quiet bungalow that yielded a surprising payload of Rolos, but don’t bother with the big, well-manicured property on the corner where only Brach’s Jelly Nougats are on offer
Such impressions sometimes became sufficiently evocative— the Rolo house —to characterize a street’s residences at other times of the year
Kids’ hauls at each house are bigger than ever, but also more similar
Back when the seasonal candy was more diverse, it communicated something about the trick-or-treatee’s aesthetics and even their values
Hershey’s bars or Tootsie Roll Pops suggested traditionalism
So did shortened tubes of Necco wafers (in an esoteric way), or cellophane-wrapped, spherical hard candies (in an antiquated one)
Baby Ruth or Butterfinger insinuated indulgence, moderated—Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups meant it immoderately
A miniature box of Nerds or a Blow Pop would have come across as progressive, at least during my youth

A packet of Pop Rocks would have felt positively punk rock. [ Read: A Halloween myth that can finally die ] Kids might share intelligence about the house offering Boston Baked Beans (actually good, but considered undesirable by peers) or Red Hots (symbolically righteous but actually underwhelming)
A handful of Sixlets—previously unheard-of—implied a larger universe than a pre-internet child might have imagined possible
Some houses matched a kid’s unexplained taste in quiet, affirming ways
For me, Spree was a peculiar pleasure, and Chuckles jelly candies, and 3 Musketeers bars, with their gentle, whipped nougat
Some doors suggested eccentricity or extremism
Even after the razor-blade panic and Tylenol scare, some homes still gave out plastic-wrapped, homemade popcorn balls, an earnest but unwelcome attempt to retain the disappearing past
Dentists sometimes offered pencils or crayons instead of candy, for obvious reasons
My parents insisted on throwing handfuls of nickels into awaiting pillowcases, a practice that caused me enormous shame despite the fact that some neighborhood children appreciated it
This opportunity to express distinctiveness at the Halloween stoop, and to receive it, has become much harder
In part, that’s because trick-or-treating has declined in general

The reasons are many: The total number of trick-or-treat-age children has decreased by a quarter since 1970; community trunk-or-treats or school events in the days leading up to Halloween started supplanting the door-to-door tradition; parents and kids decamp for “better” neighborhoods, whose betterness begets ever-increasing Hallows’ Eve inequity
Neighborhoods are less connected in general, and some municipalities enforce nanny-state ordinances around the practice
Like soda or fast food, candy was largely regional until well beyond the middle of the century
The Oh Henry! Bar, for example, was invented around 1920, by one account named after an exclamation a clerk at George Williamson’s Chicago candy store uttered to a frequent patron named Henry
But consolidation came to the candy industry
Hershey bought Reese’s in 1963, then Almond Joy and others
Mars ended up with M&M’s, Snickers, Twix, Milky Way, and many more
These days, those two companies account for around two thirds of the U.S. chocolate market
Along the way, products such as Oh Henry! fell by the wayside
That bar changed hands four times from 1965 to 2019, when it was taken off the market in the United States
Now no American child needs to ask a parent what the heck an Oh Henry! bar is, because they definitely won’t receive one in their plastic jack-o’-lantern
October retail flyers of the past reveal much greater choices
In 1970 and 1985 , Kmart advertised bags of Milk Duds, Whoppers, Dots, Sugar Daddy, Good & Plenty, and Junior Mints, among others

A 1988 coupon ad from the Leaf candy company (once the fourth-largest North American confectioner, most of whose brands were bought by Hershey in 1996) sold packs of Chuckles (my heart!), Slo Poke, Good & Fruity, Zagnut, and Rain-Blo bubble gum

Even products from companies that have survived brand acquisitions used to be more varied: Hershey’s Kisses were a common trick-or-treat offering, for example, and Tootsie Roll Industries sold bags of Tootsie Roll Pops
Now, at my local supermarket, Haribo Goldbears represent the sole independent exception

title: This Year’s Best Horror Movies Go Beyond Jump Scares
excerpt: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession
body: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession
Horror has been a particularly vital playground in the movie world of late
As studios make fewer and fewer mid-budget dramas and comedies, major names such as Jordan Peele and Ari Aster have made inroads via low-budget horror
Recently, promising new filmmakers (along with some more established veterans) have come out with an especially exciting crop of movies in this genre
I haven’t written about many of them yet, so here are my 10 favorite horror flicks from this year thus far, presented in reverse order. 10
Buffet Infinity (streaming on Shudder and AMC+) This is one of the strangest entries I’ll be recommending, but it’s a fascinating movie to throw on at home
Simon Glassman’s debut film imitates the experience of a local TV broadcast, playing out as a series of commercials and news segments with an ’80s aesthetic

At first, it’s all cheap fuzzy graphics, tinny music, and useless-sounding products, but as the movie goes on, a plot begins to emerge—inexplicable events are happening in Westridge County, Alberta, where rival businesses work around a mysterious sinkhole within which something evil may lurk
It’s a bit of a challenge to latch on to, but if you can get on its wavelength, the creepy ending is very rewarding. 9
Hokum (streaming on Hulu and Disney+) I have really enjoyed the work of the Irish horror-meister Damian McCarthy
His first two films, Caveat and Oddity , were low-budget tidbits of modern folk horror that were effective and spooky
Hokum has the same vibe on a slightly bigger scale, starring Adam Scott as a cynical writer who shacks up at a countryside hotel in Ireland to finish what he intends to be his final novel
Guess what? The hotel is haunted! But it’s haunted in a fun and peculiar way, with multiple beautifully designed scares built into its architecture

Although Hokum has one too many plots (there’s a whole strand of the protagonist’s backstory that should have been completely excised), the film has some truly creative thrills in its high-octane final act. 8
Obsession (streaming on Peacock) I confess: The box-office phenomenon that is Obsession caught me by surprise this summer
The director, Curry Barker, who was previously known for his YouTube skits, has created a wily piece of horror with a darkly comic twist
The protagonist wishes his crush loved him more than anyone; quickly, that turns into a never-ending nightmare as she pursues him with monstrous intensity

The film works, I think, because Inde Navarrette’s performance as the supernaturally “obsessed” Nikki is so sympathetic, but I found the movie more unpleasant and discomforting than scary on my first viewing
It went on to make more than $500 million (roughly 500 times what it cost to produce) and will be getting a major Oscar campaign, so I probably owe it a second viewing. 7
It Ends (available for rent online) I reviewed It Ends when it was released in August, and still think quite highly of it
It’s another low-budget indie that does an exceptional job stretching its dollar to maximize its scares, which are mostly of the existential sort
The film follows a group of friends who get stuck driving on a road they can’t get off of, frozen in a weird limbo that makes them all go mad in differing ways
Where some indies find innovative approaches to gore and others lean into shocking jump scares, It Ends sources terror from mounting dread and aimless uncertainty. 6
Exit 8 (streaming on Shudder and AMC+) Liminal horror has become the latest trend in the genre, and video-game adaptations are also all the rage

The Japanese film Exit 8 delivers both, re-creating a well-received adventure game in which the player is trapped in an eerie, endlessly repeating subway station with no way out and a confusing puzzle to solve

Imposing a narrative on something so vague and mysterious can be challenging, but the director Genki Kawamura does that well, effectively using this bizarre scenario as a metaphor for his protagonist feeling stuck on a major life decision
Be warned, though—things get pretty yucky by the end. 5

Backrooms (streaming on HBO Max) The most popular liminal-horror hit of the summer was the adaptation of a viral YouTube series from the distressingly young Kane Parsons (who was, no kidding, 20 years old when he made it)
Backrooms was such a box-office success that studios are now scrambling to copy it, snapping up the rights to every spooky “creepypasta” video they can find

But I think the movie will not be so easily imitated; it’s effective because of Parsons’s incredible control of mood and tone through his production design and visual effects, throwing the viewer and his characters into weird, looping hallways and jumbled-together office spaces that feel like half-remembered dreams. 4
Resident Evil (in theaters now) Even though this is yet another video-game adaptation, Resident Evil takes a big swing at the most famous horror-video-game intellectual property that exists
Zach Cregger (who has become a huge name in the horror genre) constructed a film that is intense, action-packed, and very creative with its CGI gore

But I like it most of all because it captures the sweaty experience of gaming, making its hero (played by Austin Abrams) a lovable avatar for any of us who’ve struggled through waves of zombie attacks on our consoles at home. 3

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (streaming on MUBI) Jane Schoenbrun’s knowing satire is a horror movie about horror movies, particularly the ways that both corporate studios and devoted fans try to remake and reinterpret them for new generations

This film succeeds by never feeling too academic or self-reflexive, partly because of its sharp script and partly because of the outstanding chemistry between its leads: Hannah Einbinder, who plays a young filmmaker obsessed with a moribund slasher franchise, and Gillian Anderson as that franchise’s reclusive, retired lead actor. 2
Chronovisor (in select theaters now) This movie has been the find of the year for me

It’s a bizarre debut from Jack Auen and Kevin Walker about an academic who stumbles across an odd urban legend in her research, a “time viewer” that allows the viewer to see events from the past (such as the Crucifixion)

As she delves deeper and deeper into the writing on this topic, the texts she’s reading flash on-screen, along with snippets of videos; it’s like a found-footage movie, but most of the footage has been written down. (Trust me, it’s spookier than it sounds.) The ending is impossible to describe and a wonder to behold

The movie is touring around the country right now —if you can catch it in a cinema, I can guarantee a unique viewing experience. 1. 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (streaming on Netflix) For me, no horror movie has quite compared with the thrilling rush I got from seeing Nia DaCosta’s entry in the 28 Days Later series

The Bone Temple is a sequel to Danny Boyle’s excellent 28 Years Later , centering on that film’s best supporting character, a kindly doctor named Ian Kelson (Ralph Fiennes) who is cultivating a sculptural memorial to the Rage Virus’s victims decades after the pathogen turned Britain into a zombie apocalypse

title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test
body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test
They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded
Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website
It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI
In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track

And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts
That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time

But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.  Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes
That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems
In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it
And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not

They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions
So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks
This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit
We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures
Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks
This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.  The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed
Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions

The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans
The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision
In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took

And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible

The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized
The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory
And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging

The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used

No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.  AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory

Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules
Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry

We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.  No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong
Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this
And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable

title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
excerpt: A dangerous blind spot in climate models: Current models used to inform major UN climate reports fail to account for powerful feedback loops—where warming itsel
body: A dangerous blind spot in climate models: Current models used to inform major UN climate reports fail to account for powerful feedback loops—where warming itself drives more warming—leaving us underestimating how fast temperatures could rise
The numbers are alarming: Thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, warming wetlands and other feedbck effects could add 0.2°C to 0.4°C of extra warming this century

Scientists are scrambling to catch up: Over 20 international research teams are now running coordinated analyses to better understand these feedback effects, with hopes the UN will incorporate findings into its next major climate assessment in 2029. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147735" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change

Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be
And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century
That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100

The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.  None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects

That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March , which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed

It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects

Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.  At least some of this is starting to happen

Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project , through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power
Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029
That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution

And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.  So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control

Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story )

In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.  Several startups are also exploring possibilities

They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile

But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.  The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.  This article is from The Spark,  MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday,   sign up here .

title: What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?
url:
<title>What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768629/original/file-20261027-52-uhinol.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">For Muslims, Sharia refers to the divinely guided principles of living a moral life.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/sharia-law-gavel-and-holy-koran-on-blue-background-royalty-free-image/2256988748?phrase=%20sharia%20&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">sean zheng lim/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>At a <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/25/trump-escalates-campaign-rhetoric-calling-el-sayed-jihadist/">campaign rally</a>, in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026, President Donald Trump accused U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of being a “jihadist” who wants to impose Sharia law – Islamic law – in the United States. His comments reflect a broader pattern among Republican politicians of portraying Sharia as a threat to the American legal system.</p>

<p>In March 2026, Texas legislators launched the Sharia Free Texas Caucus, a group dedicated to preventing what its members describe as the spread of Islamic law in Texas. Its founder, state Rep. Brent Money, has characterized Sharia as “an entire civilizational legal structure” that threatens American law and institutions. That same month, <a href="https://ktvz.com/politics/cnn-us-politics/2026/04/11/its-solid-gold-some-texas-republicans-ramp-up-criticisms-of-muslims-to-energize-primary-voters/">nearly 95% of Texas Republican primary voters</a> backed a nonbinding proposition declaring that “<a href="https://www.tarrantcountytx.gov/content/dam/main/elections/2026/pm26/Republican_Party_Props.pdf">Texas should prohibit Sharia Law</a>.” The movement extends beyond Texas. In Congress, the <a href="https://keithself.house.gov/media/press-releases/congressman-self-and-congressman-roys-sharia-free-america-caucus-grows-68">Sharia Free America Caucus</a>, established in December 2025, grew to 68 Republican lawmakers from 25 states in just six months.</p>

<p>These efforts reflect a <a href="https://bridge.georgetown.edu/research/whats-wrong-with-the-march-against-sharia/">long-standing claim</a>, frequently invoked by anti-Sharia activists, that Muslims are seeking to establish a parallel legal system that will eventually replace American law.</p>

<p>But this rhetoric raises a more basic question: What exactly is Sharia, and what does it actually mean for Muslims to follow it while living in the United States?</p>

<p>I am a <a href="https://law.msu.edu/faculty-staff/u/asma-t-uddin">law professor who studies religious liberty</a>. My 2019 book, “<a href="https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/When-Islam-is-Not-a-Religion/Asma-T-Uddin/9781643136059">When Islam Is Not a Religion</a>,” examined how ordinary Muslim religious practices come to be treated as political threats, and I recently <a href="https://theconversation.com/in-texas-ordinary-muslim-religious-practices-are-increasingly-being-treated-as-political-threats-290219">documented that pattern in Texas</a>. The Sharia controversy shows how this happens.</p>

<h2>Sharia is not a single legal code</h2>

<p>In Arabic, “sharia” means a path or way, literally “<a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Shariah">the path to a watering place</a>.” For Muslims, it refers to the divinely ordained way of living a moral and religious life, guided by the Quran and the teachings of the Prophet Muhammad.</p>

<p>Sharia guides Muslims how to pray, when to fast, what to eat and how much to give to charity. It also addresses marriage and divorce. These rules span what Americans would sort into law, ethics, manners and worship, as law professor and an authority on Islamic law <a href="https://law.wisc.edu/profiles/asifa.quraishi-landes">Asifa Quraishi-Landes</a> has <a href="https://religionnews.com/2017/06/08/how-anti-shariah-marches-mistake-muslim-concepts-of-state-and-religious-law/">explained</a>.</p>

<p>This distinction matters because Americans often think of law as something established and enforced by the state. Sharia is broader than that. A Muslim who avoids pork or prays five times a day may see each practice as part of following Sharia, but neither requires a separate legal court or government enforcement. </p>

<p>Rules governing marriage, divorce and inheritance, by contrast, may have legal consequences, though how they are interpreted and applied varies across Islamic traditions. Indeed, as Quraishi-Landes notes, Sharia itself <a href="https://kuow.org/stories/want-argue-about-sharia-heres-what-it-means">obliges Muslims to follow the law of the land</a> wherever they live.</p>

<h2>Who decides what Sharia requires?</h2>

<p>Muslims do not all agree on how Sharia should be interpreted. They distinguish between Sharia, which they regard as the divine ideal, and “<a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/fiqh">fiqh,” the human effort to understand and apply it</a>. In other words, Muslims believe Sharia comes from God, but people must figure out what it requires in practice. Because people can disagree, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1163/19585705-12341457">interpretations can differ</a> and change over time.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

              <span class="caption">For Muslims, Sharia is an expression of divine guidance.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-indonesian-muslim-man-reads-the-koran-at-istiqlal-grand-news-photo/104076673?phrase=woman%20reading%20the%20%20quran&amp;adppopup=true">Bay Ismoyo/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Sunni Islam’s four major schools and Shiite Islam’s legal traditions sometimes reach different conclusions about matters such as marriage, divorce and financial transactions. </p>

<p>For example, scholars differ on <a href="https://fiqhcouncil.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/FCNA-Fatwas-Compiled-November-2022.doc.pdf">whether Muslims can take out conventional mortgages</a> to buy homes, given Islamic prohibitions on interest, and on the conditions under which a marriage can be dissolved. They continue to debate newer questions, too, such as <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7056282/">whether organ donation is permissible</a> or how <a href="https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s43093-026-01002-5">modern banking can comply with Islamic principles</a>.</p>

<p>No single institution speaks for all Muslims. Yet political debates often treat Sharia as a fixed rule book, when much of the Islamic legal tradition consists of ongoing disagreements about what its rules mean and how they should apply.</p>

<h2>How does Sharia work in the US?</h2>

<p>Muslims are subject to the same laws as everyone else in the United States. Their religious commitments may guide personal decisions about marriage, divorce, finances and everyday conduct, but Sharia has no independent legal authority. Muslims can follow religious rules voluntarily, but those rules cannot override American law.</p>

<p>This is not unique to Islam. Religious communities across the country have long used their own procedures to resolve disputes. For example, many Orthodox Jewish couples sign <a href="https://www.jofa.org/article/the-pre-nuptial-agreement-for-the-prevention-of-get-refusal/">prenuptial agreements</a> committing them to appear before a Jewish religious court, known as a beth din, if their marriage breaks down. The court can then help facilitate a religious divorce, including addressing situations in which a husband refuses to grant his wife a religious divorce. Christian organizations likewise offer <a href="https://www.aorhope.org/icc">biblical mediation and arbitration</a> to resolve conflicts according to religious principles.</p>

<p>Muslims can similarly turn to religious scholars or mediators for guidance on family or financial disputes. These arrangements are generally voluntary, and any legally enforceable agreement must comply with American law. </p>

<p>A religious ruling does not become binding simply because a religious authority issues it. Like other religious communities, Muslims may organize aspects of their personal lives around their faith, but they do so within the framework of American law.</p>

<h2>Can American courts enforce Sharia?</h2>

<p>Critics often claim Sharia is gaining a foothold in the courts. The concern usually arises when Muslims ask a court to recognize a religious contract or arbitration.</p>

<p>Consider an Islamic marriage contract promising the wife a marriage gift, known as “mahr,” some or all of which may be payable if the couple divorces. A court asked to enforce it does not decide what Islamic theology requires. It asks whether the agreement meets ordinary contract law. In 2020, a Maryland appeals court held that a “mahr” <a href="https://www.mdcourts.gov/data/opinions/cosa/2020/0585s18.pdf">could be enforced only under the same secular standards</a> that apply to any agreement between spouses. In other words, the court’s job is to determine whether the couple’s agreement is legally enforceable, just as it would with any other contract. It is not enforcing Islamic religious law.</p>

<p>Courts may apply what the Supreme Court calls “<a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/443/595">neutral principles of law</a>.” That simply means applying ordinary legal rules without deciding religious questions. A judge can determine whether two people entered into a valid contract, for example, but cannot decide which interpretation of Islam is religiously correct. As <a href="https://www.law.uc.edu/faculty/directory/DeanHaiderAlaHamoudi.html">law professor Haider Ala Hamoudi</a> <a href="https://islamiclaw.blog/2017/09/05/the-irony-of-sharia-bans-part-i/">has observed</a>, courts can enforce a “mahr” agreement precisely because doing so does not require them to interpret Islamic law.</p>

<p>Arbitration works the same way. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has called Islamic panels “<a href="https://mediate.com/news/texas-ag-paxton-demands-documents-from-islamic-tribunal-a-dallas-faith-based-mediation-group/">Sharia tribunals masquerading as legal courts</a>.” Yet the Beth Din of America also <a href="https://bethdin.org/dintorah">structures its proceedings</a> so civil courts can enforce its rulings, as do Christian arbitrators. </p>

<p>Courts can enforce voluntary arbitration awards and <a href="https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._civ._practice_and_remedies_code_section_171.088">can also vacate them</a> for fraud or overreach. For example, suppose a Muslim couple voluntarily agree to have a religious arbitrator resolve a financial dispute. If the arbitrator orders one spouse to pay the other US$10,000, a court may enforce that decision just as it would any other arbitration award. But if one spouse was coerced into participating or the arbitrator exceeded the authority the couple had agreed to give them, a court could set the decision aside.</p>

<p>A religious arbitrator cannot override a statute or the Constitution.</p>

<h2>Why is Sharia so controversial?</h2>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some concerns stem from how certain governments enforce Islamic law. In Iran, U.N. investigators have documented <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2024/09/1154306">escalating violence against women</a> accused of violating hijab rules. In Afghanistan, the Taliban have issued <a href="https://www.thestar.com.my/news/world/2026/08/13/half-of-afghan-women-rarely-leave-home-as-taliban-restrictions-deepen-un-agency-says">more than 100 decrees targeting women and girls</a>.</p>

<p>These policies raise serious questions about religious coercion, gender equality and freedom of conscience. Muslim scholars and reformers have long <a href="https://warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/law/elj/lgd/2010_1/br_akhtar/">debated those questions themselves</a>. One example is <a href="https://www.international.ucla.edu/ccs/article/105896">Musawah</a>, an international movement founded in Malaysia in 2009 that advocates equality and justice in Muslim family laws. Working with scholars and activists across the world, it argues that Islamic teachings can support women’s rights and challenges discriminatory interpretations of religious law.</p>

<p>American debates often collapse these issues into one question: whether Sharia itself is compatible with American law. That framing obscures a crucial distinction. A government imposing religious rules on unwilling citizens is doing something fundamentally different from an individual choosing to follow them. A Muslim woman who wears a hijab is not asking the government to mandate religious dress. </p>

<h2>The American campaign against Sharia</h2>

<p>Between 2010 and 2012, lawmakers in <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2013/04/08/state-legislation-restricting-use-of-foreign-or-religious-law/">at least 32 states</a> introduced bills to keep courts from applying Sharia or foreign law.</p>

<p>In 2010, Oklahoma voters approved a constitutional amendment barring courts from considering Sharia. A federal appeals court <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca10/10-6273/10-6273-2012-01-10.html">upheld an injunction</a> against the amendment, finding that it likely violated the First Amendment’s protection of religious freedom by singling out Islam for unfavorable treatment. In 2013, a federal judge <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/oklahomas-shariah-law-ban-is-unconstitutional-gone-for-good/">struck it down permanently</a>.</p>

<p>Other states adopted broader bans on the use of foreign law. Supporters say these measures protect women’s rights. Critics argue that they address a <a href="https://www.jurist.org/commentary/2015/03/steven-schwinn-sharia-law/">problem American law already guards against</a>: Courts cannot enforce agreements that violate fundamental legal protections.</p>

<p>For example, a court can reject an agreement obtained through coercion or fraud, or one that violates a person’s constitutional rights or other applicable laws. Those protections apply regardless of whether an agreement is based on religious principles.</p>

<p>The effort has now reached Congress: In June 2026, U.S. Rep. Keith Self of Texas introduced a bill to <a href="https://dallasexpress.com/column/texas-sounded-the-alarm-now-will-we-act/">bar federal courts from enforcing foreign or religious laws</a> that conflict with the Constitution. But courts already cannot enforce agreements that violate the Constitution or other applicable laws. The proposed restriction thus raises a basic question: What additional protection would it provide?</p>

<p>The central point is that American law already provides safeguards against religious rules being imposed through the courts. Muslims, like members of other faiths, can organize their personal lives around their religious beliefs. But those beliefs do not carry independent legal authority, and courts cannot enforce them in ways that violate applicable American law.</p>

<p>The debate over Sharia is not just about religious law. It is also about whether Americans are willing to extend the same understanding of religious freedom to Muslims that they extend to other faiths.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294224/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Political information increasingly comes from pop culture, outside of partisan silos but where male creators – and sometimes misogyny – dominate</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768599/original/file-20261027-92-7x0z47.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=487%2C0%2C4197%2C2798&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Young people are increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers and popular culture sources.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/social-media-platforms-abstract-desk-working-royalty-free-illustration/2193464406?phrase=pop%20culture%20podcasts%20influencers&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Illustration JDawnInk/Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Research on political polarization points to how people’s <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2025/06/10/the-political-gap-in-americans-news-sources/">preferred news outlets</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/acrefore/9780190228613.013.1523">social media use</a> create information silos, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsis.2025.101904">environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own</a>, further cementing those views.  </p>

<p>But this research often omits an important source of political information: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12115-016-0053-1">popular culture</a>, from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies.</p>

<p><a href="https://lsupress.org/9780807170342/politics-for-the-love-of-fandom/">Politics are intertwined with popular entertainment media</a>. The current president is a former reality television star who was reelected in 2024 with the help of <a href="https://www.vulture.com/article/donald-trump-andrew-schulz-flagrant-theo-von-podcast-interviews.html">comedy podcasters like Joe Rogan</a>. Blockbuster films such as “The Odyssey” <a href="https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20260626-why-the-odyssey-has-caused-so-much-controversy">spark controversy</a> and turn into <a href="https://theconversation.com/elon-musk-says-ai-will-make-a-historically-accurate-odyssey-heres-why-thats-impossible-288333">political footballs</a>, while <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/trump-administration/jimmy-kimmel-abc-tv-show-wont-air-james-talarico-interview-fcc-threats-rcna596994">late-night talk show hosts must skirt</a> the Trump administration’s regulatory ire with their politically oriented humor.</p>

<p>While we know a lot about <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2025/06/10/the-political-gap-in-americans-news-sources/">the news-consumption habits of Republicans and Democrats</a>, there is less data about the other places that people encounter political ideas. This is particularly true for younger people, who are <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/news-influencers-fact-sheet/">increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers</a> and <a href="https://opensquare.nyupress.org/books/9781479829712/">popular culture sources</a>.</p>

<p>Political consultant Sarah Longwell of The Bulwark <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-sarah-longwell.html">recently told The New York Times’ Ezra Klein</a> that many people in her focus groups get political information from an “algorithm-driven information environment” populated by influencers, comedians and sports personalities. She noted that the “overlap between politics and culture” creates a “vibe” that shapes many people’s political decision-making. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://communicationstudies.colostate.edu/cdapc/about/">co-founders and research affiliates</a> of Colorado State University’s <a href="https://communicationstudies.colostate.edu/cdapc/">Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture</a>, we conducted a survey that documents the pop culture preferences of Americans ages 18-49. </p>

<p>We wanted to know whether the siloing that has been observed in Americans’ news environments is replicated when younger Americans are consuming entertainment media that often contains political content. </p>

<p>It isn’t.</p>

<p>That matters, because popular influencers and entertainers who cross partisan boundaries have an increased ability to shape the political “vibe” discussed by Longwell. And an important finding from our survey is that many of the favorite creators and outlets ranked in the survey feature men and promote masculinity.</p>

<h2>Favorite influencers and podcasts</h2>

<p><a href="https://sociology.as.virginia.edu/sites/sociology.as.virginia.edu/files/2023-04/Popular%20Culture%20-%20Oxford%20Reference.pdf">Pop culture</a> is the diverse collection of cultural productions consumed by members of a society: films, television series, video games, art, music, comedy and the like. </p>

<p>We asked 741 Americans to name their top influencers, podcasts, comedians, musicians, video games, films and television series. We examined results by age and political party.</p>

<p>Respondents first identified which pop culture outlets they engaged with and then shared their favorites in each content category. The answers were diffuse, but trends are evident in the top three listed by people across political affiliations.</p>

<p>Both the <a href="https://www.wired.com/story/influencer-takeover-dnc/">Democratic</a> and <a href="https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/politics-news/trump-wins-influencer-election-1236055439/">Republican</a> parties have <a href="https://www.npr.org/2024/09/01/nx-s1-5091076/dnc-content-creators-influencers-convention-tiktok-instagram">turned to influencers to reach voters – particularly young voters</a> – who “don’t consume traditional political news.”</p>

<p>In our survey’s lists of favorite influencers, three creators who rose to fame staging viral stunts, interviewing celebrities and playing video games on YouTube and <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Twitch-service">the live streaming platform Twitch</a> dominated the list: <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/MrBeast">MrBeast</a> was No. 1 for Democrats, Republicans and independents. Republicans and independents ranked <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZlekAB6oP8">Kai Cenat</a> in their top three, while <a href="https://www.imdb.com/name/nm12964938/bio/">IShowSpeed</a> was No. 2 for Democrats and Republicans.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A chart showing pictures of the top 3 favorite influencers by political party -- Republicans, Democrats and independents" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=750&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=750&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=750&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767134/original/file-20261020-50-b2jao0.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The top three favorite influencers by political affiliation  – Republicans, Democrats and independents.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A similar pattern of the same names populating each list is evident in people’s favorite podcasts. “<a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Joe-Rogan">The Joe Rogan Experience</a>” and “<a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Alex-Cooper#ref1342804">Call Her Daddy</a>” were in all groups’ top three, while Republicans and independents also ranked the “<a href="https://tuckercarlson.com/">Tucker Carlson Show</a>” and “<a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Theo-Von">This Past Weekend with Theo Von</a>.” </p>

<p>Joe Rogan and Theo Von are <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-liberals-lost-comedy-and-helped-trump-win-244380">comedians turned podcasters</a>, whereas Tucker Carlson rose to fame as a right-wing pundit. “Call Her Daddy” is an outlier on our list insofar as it is hosted by a woman, Alex Cooper, and is known for frank discussions of sex and relationships.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A chart showing pictures of the top three favorite podcasts by political party." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=750&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=750&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=750&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767135/original/file-20261020-50-tdy94f.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=943&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>The website Campaigns &amp; Elections reported that in 2024 half of all registered voters surveyed who listened to at least one podcast per month said that <a href="https://campaignsandelections.com/industry-news/podcasts-played-pivotal-role-in-2024-election/">podcasts had some influence on their vote</a>. The site reported that in the 2024 presidential election, those podcast listeners favored conservatives.</p>

<p>Our survey helps to explain why. Rogan, popular with all three groups, has long voiced <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-liberals-lost-comedy-and-helped-trump-win-244380">libertarian ideas and platformed right-wing politicians</a>. Von occupies a similar space, and Carlson is conservative. Both are favorites not just of Republicans but also independents.</p>

<h2>Favorite comedians and video games</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/s41296-020-00451-z">Political scientists</a> and <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/thats-not-funny/paper">media scholars</a> have demonstrated how comedy can influence politics. Our survey found considerable overlap among political partisans’ favorite comedians.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0152638/">Dave Chappelle</a>, creator of the boundary-breaking Comedy Central series “Chappelle’s Show,” topped the list for Democrats and Republicans and was the second favorite of independents. Bill Burr, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2013/11/08/arts/bill-burrs-irate-comedy-style.html">known for comedy that is both cocky and aggrieved</a>, was in the top three for Republicans and Democrats, while Shane Gillis, whose comedy The New York Times says “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2023/09/16/arts/television/shane-gillis-beautiful-dogs-netflix-comedy.html">fits into the evolving meaning of conservatism</a>,” was second and third for independents and Republicans. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>Video games are another shared pop culture venue where Americans of different political affiliations are encountering one another as they play, via discussions with other players on Twitch and by participating in the comments sections of gameplay livestreams. </p>

<p>Researchers have demonstrated that young people, in particular, are exposed to diverse political views when engaging with one another in “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/20563051211008821">online participatory activities that are non-political in nature</a>.”</p>

<p>For example, one study examined how a viral trend of “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/20563051211008821">building Trump’s wall” while playing Fortnite spurred political discussions</a> both inside the game and in comments on gameplay videos and social media posts.</p>

<p>U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez demonstrated the political power of the medium in 2020 when she livestreamed herself playing the game Among Us, an online, multiplayer deduction game similar to the popular party games <a href="https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgamefamily/2989/game-werewolf-mafia">Mafia and Werewolf</a>. Ocasio-Cortez playing the game with <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/21/tech/aoc-twitch-account-voting">U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar and prominent gamers</a> was billed as a get-out-the-vote effort and earned 4.5 million views.</p>

<p>In our survey of video games favored by people of different political affiliations, Call of Duty, Fortnite and Sims appeared on all three lists.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our data suggests that these pop culture spaces are thus not partisan silos. But that doesn’t mean they are free of particular ideologies. </p>

<h2>Manosphere vibes</h2>

<p>Some of the most popular creators – Rogan, Von, Carlson and Gillis – <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/06/arts/music/theo-von-andrew-schulz-joe-rogan-manosphere-popcast.html">appeal to, or helped construct</a>, the <a href="https://theconversation.com/youd-better-start-paying-attention-to-the-manosphere-youre-living-in-it-279547">manosphere</a>, a loose collection of online communities that promote masculinity and often reflect misogynistic attitudes. </p>

<p>Burr’s comedy is not politically conservative. But The New York Times <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2013/11/08/arts/bill-burrs-irate-comedy-style.html">said that it</a> “gives voice to the aggrieved confusion of the white heterosexual guy adrift.”</p>

<p>Chappelle is known for his <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1041794X.2020.1797146">satirical critiques of racism</a>. But in his more recent Netflix stand-up specials, he voiced <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/chappelle-special-draws-critics-boosters-to-netflix-walkout">anti-trans</a> <a href="https://www.huffpost.com/entry/dave-chappelle-trans-jokes-republican-transphobia_n_69e140f2e4b0b6f552b8410e">sentiments</a> <a href="https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/04/chappelle-anti-trans-transphobic-gop-republican-comedy-boebert/">that Mother Jones called</a> “indistinguishable from, and grist for, the material of conservative streamers and right-wing edgelords.”</p>

<p>Our survey did not ask respondents why they preferred these influencers, podcasts, comedians and video games. Academic research has shown that pop culture audiences <a href="https://doi.org/10.4135/9781446221280.n1">don’t passively accept every message a creator delivers</a>. Nevertheless, the dominance of male creators and the prevalence of misogyny and transphobia in their humor and commentary is significant.</p>

<p>Whether convened online or in person, the groups that gather via popular culture do not fit into the partisan silos that have formed around news and social media outlets. That makes the gendered nature of these lists even more significant, because the manosphere vibes are not relegated to one side of the political spectrum.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294202/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
