Illustration JDawnInk/Getty Images Plus Research on political polarization points to how people’s preferred news outlets and social media use create information silos, environments in which people primarily encounter views consistent with their own , further cementing those views
But this research often omits an important source of political information: popular culture , from influencers and podcasts to comedy, television and movies
Politics are intertwined with popular entertainment media
The current president is a former reality television star who was reelected in 2024 with the help of comedy podcasters like Joe Rogan

Blockbuster films such as “The Odyssey” spark controversy and turn into political footballs , while late-night talk show hosts must skirt the Trump administration’s regulatory ire with their politically oriented humor
While we know a lot about the news-consumption habits of Republicans and Democrats , there is less data about the other places that people encounter political ideas
This is particularly true for younger people, who are increasingly likely to get political content from social media influencers and popular culture sources

Political consultant Sarah Longwell of The Bulwark recently told The New York Times’ Ezra Klein that many people in her focus groups get political information from an “algorithm-driven information environment” populated by influencers, comedians and sports personalities
She noted that the “overlap between politics and culture” creates a “vibe” that shapes many people’s political decision-making

As co-founders and research affiliates of Colorado State University’s Center for Democracy, Art, and Popular Culture , we conducted a survey that documents the pop culture preferences of Americans ages 18-49

We wanted to know whether the siloing that has been observed in Americans’ news environments is replicated when younger Americans are consuming entertainment media that often contains political content
That matters, because popular influencers and entertainers who cross partisan boundaries have an increased ability to shape the political “vibe” discussed by Longwell
And an important finding from our survey is that many of the favorite creators and outlets ranked in the survey feature men and promote masculinity

We asked 741 Americans to name their top influencers, podcasts, comedians, musicians, video games, films and television series

Respondents first identified which pop culture outlets they engaged with and then shared their favorites in each content category

<title>Democrats are the unwitting beneficiaries of Trump’s immigration policies</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768799/original/file-20261028-52-89c023.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5122%2C3414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A volunteer walks along the U.S.-Mexico border near Jacumba Hot Springs, Calif., on June 5, 2025.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/USMexicoBorderImmigration/870dcafddf4048409f7f89274301995d/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=US%20border%20crossing&amp;currentItemNo=8&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Gregory Bull</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>In <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/07/us/politics/biden-immigration-trump.html">a 2025 investigation</a>, The New York Times reported that officials in President Joe Biden’s administration, in the wake of Biden’s 2020 election win, had viewed rising immigration as “a distraction” best ignored so that the administration could concentrate political resources on more important economic matters. </p>

<p>Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was “wishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about.”</p>

<p>But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administration’s <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/26/trump-closed-down-border-ended-it-campaign-issue/">management of the U.S. southern border</a> to <a href="https://rollcall.com/2024/11/06/trump-win-opens-door-to-major-shift-in-us-immigration-policies/">win the 2024 election</a> and enforce his <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/23/ag-leaders-say-trumps-immigration-crackdown-is-disrupting-us-food-supply/">immigration crackdown</a>, the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.</p>

<p>Amid the <a href="https://www.urban.org/data-tools/american-affordability-tracker">rising U.S. cost of living</a>, a <a href="https://apnews.com/article/iran-war-trump-economy-oil-gas-66806b02a000235f1979e591279b6554">destabilizing war in Iran</a> and a <a href="https://www.weforum.org/stories/financial-and-monetary-systems/understanding-fragmented-global-financial-system-safeguarding-its-integrity">disrupted system of global commerce</a>, <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/residents-border-towns-relieved-quiet-record-low-migrant-crossings-rcna236200">the now-quiet border</a> has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections. </p>

<h2>From liability to advantage</h2>

<p>For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.</p>

<p>Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/immigration-reform-failure-congress-timeline-rcna64467">2006, 2007 and 2013</a>. Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.</p>

<p>In a February 2024 poll, 28% of <a href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/611135/immigration-surges-top-important-problem-list.aspx">U.S. respondents told Gallup</a> that immigration was the country’s most important problem – matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period. </p>

<p>In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U.S. registered voters who identified immigration as the country’s most important issue fell from <a href="https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/econTabReport_NgtZTja.pdf">14% in October 2024</a> to <a href="https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/econTabReport_CCphJ5Q.pdf">5% in September 2026</a>.</p>

<p>Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have <a href="https://www.axios.com/2026/10/01/trump-immigration-midterms-polling-economy">reduced the urgency of immigration</a>, depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage. </p>

<p>“You become a victim of your own success,” he said.</p>

<p>But this success is dubious. President Trump’s approval ratings on immigration are underwater.</p>

<p>In the <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/approval/donald-trump/issues/immigration">RealClear Polling average</a> from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10.8%. In a recent <a href="https://www.foxnews.com/politics/fox-news-poll-majority-says-immigration-enforcement-has-crossed-line">Fox News poll</a>, most Americans believe the Trump administration has “gone too far” in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.</p>

<p>Despite Republicans’ insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2024/11/22/business/economy/immigration-trump-economy.html">raise wages</a> and <a href="https://katv.com/news/nation-world/white-house-says-mass-deportations-are-lowering-housing-costs-in-the-us-san-diego-illegal-migrants-texas-florida">make housing more accessible</a>, Americans are experiencing <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/26/trump-second-term-economy-charts">high inflation rates</a>, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/30/business/economy/us-economy-gdp-growth.html">slow gross domestic product growth</a> and <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/us-consumer-sentiment-near-record-low-ahead-midterm-elections-2026-10-23/">sour consumer sentiment</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>Ominously for the White House, Trump’s negative 10.8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/approval/donald-trump/issues/inflation">negative 42.8%</a>, <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/approval/donald-trump/issues/economy">negative 31.7%</a> and <a href="https://www.realclearpolling.com/polls/approval/donald-trump/issues/foreign-policy">negative 27.8%</a>, respectively.</p>

<p>These dynamics bode well for Democrats’ midterm election prospects.</p>

<p>Republicans are now less concerned about immigration – what has been their greatest source of political energy and the left’s greatest political liability – as both parties’ voters are focused on other matters.</p>

<p>Despite the White House’s aggressive and frequently <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/08/06/the-chaos-and-cruelty-of-ice/">violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants</a>, its <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/06/supreme-court-strikes-down-trumps-order-ending-birthright-citizenship/">proposal to end birthright citizenship</a>, and its <a href="https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/national-media-release/trump-administration-delivers-11-straight-months-zero-releases">near closure of U.S. borders</a>, even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the country’s top issue today than they were previously.</p>

<p>According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.</p>

<p>Remarkably, without Democrats’ endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a <a href="https://maristpoll.marist.edu/polls/2026-midterm-elections-september-2026">September 2026 Marist survey</a>.</p>

<h2>Democrats’ trial and error</h2>

<p>Democrats’ sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.</p>

<p>Before Trump’s 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U.S., by highlighting that immigrants <a href="https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aeri.20200588">start more businesses</a>, <a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w30797">file more patents</a> and <a href="https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/aeri.20230459">commit fewer crimes</a> than native-born U.S. citizens on average. </p>

<p>During this period, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2014/nov/20/obama-speech-on-immigration-in-full">Democrats commonly cited</a> immigrants’ acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/powerpost/paloma/daily-202/2017/09/06/daily-202-daca-reaction-shows-how-immigration-has-become-a-litmus-test-for-democrats/59af142730fb04264c2a1ced">praise and pity produced resentment</a> among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.</p>

<p>Toward the end of the first Trump administration, <a href="https://democrats-budget.house.gov/resources/reports/congress-must-act-comprehensive-immigration-reform">Democrats
began citing</a> the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrants’ long-term settlement in the U.S. </p>

<p>Economists attribute to immigrants <a href="https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2017/08/30/immigrants-boost-americas-birth-rate">the bulk of U.S. population growth</a> from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that <a href="https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/america-needs-more-immigration-defeat-inflation">continued immigration mitigates inflation</a> and extends <a href="https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/immigration-social-security-solvency/">the solvency of Social Security</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-015-3418-z">Medicare funds</a>. Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/23/ag-leaders-say-trumps-immigration-crackdown-is-disrupting-us-food-supply/">agriculture</a>, food production and <a href="https://www.kff.org/immigrant-health/the-role-of-immigrants-in-the-u-s-health-care-workforce/">healthcare</a>. </p>

<p>However, the benefits of these relationships for average voters tend to be diffuse and realized in the medium-to-long run. That makes them hard to recognize.</p>

<p>After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/07/us/politics/biden-immigration-trump.html">avoid the immigration issue</a> altogether. It’s a strategy that Democrats have now carried over while the dynamics of being out of power still permit doing so.</p>

<h2>No mandate for inaction</h2>

<p>Should <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/25/nx-s1-6014525/politics-chat-the-polls-show-a-democratic-sweep-in-the-midterms-can-you-trust-them">Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives</a> in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved. As a matter of constitutional oversight, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/democrats-trump-allies-investigation-plans-c226c1fc">Democrats plan to commence investigations</a> into the Trump administration’s abusive immigration enforcement tactics, questionable case adjudication and alleged corruption. </p>

<p>It will be almost impossible to pass meaningful immigration legislation in such an environment.</p>

<p>The Biden-era approach was a pivotal electoral liability in 2024. And the Obama administration’s series of immigration executive actions instigated a tennis match of such orders between subsequent administrations ever since.</p>

<p>Democrats will soon feel some pressure to develop bipartisan approaches to immigration governance that ensure order at U.S. borders and a strategy for immigrant selection and integration that is designed with the national interest in mind.</p>

<p>Anything less, and the dysfunctional system – with its massive political risks – will return.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/295235/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>We discovered an organism that lives at blistering temperatures – but what allows it to take the heat?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766782/original/file-20261016-50-bo80qy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=6%2C0%2C4987%2C3325&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Studying organisms that survive in extreme heat, like in geothermal springs, helps scientists learn about how life adapts. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/salt-formations-in-grand-prismatic-spring-royalty-free-image/2260969480?phrase=thermophile&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Gary Yeowell/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Organisms are products of the environments they live and evolve in. While the physical world is governed by universal laws like thermodynamics and gravity, there are few laws of biology. An open question <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=F_dSX1QAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">for biologists like me</a> is how environmental conditions shape what organisms look like and dictate how they live, breathe and move.</p>

<p>Organisms can adapt to survive in a wide variety of conditions, from salty water to extreme heat or cold and changing climates. Most <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/eukaryote">eukaryotic organisms</a> that have been studied with cell types similar to our own live at <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/sdata.2018.22">temperatures close to those of the human body</a>, with an average of 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius).</p>

<p>Organisms thriving at temperatures higher than this range, known as thermophiles, could help directly answer what effect temperature has on the rules for life. These rules can help scientists learn more about where life could exist. In <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.08.043">a study published in September 2026</a>, our research team identified a new thermophile that can survive at hotter conditions than any other previously recorded.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A microscope slide showing an organism that looks like a trunk with two large, branched limbs coming off it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=461&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=461&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=461&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=579&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=579&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766764/original/file-20261016-50-fjx1da.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=579&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="caption">An amoeba is a type of eukaryotic organism that changes shape as it moves. Shown here is <em>Amoeba proteus</em>.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amoeba_%28genus%29#/media/File:Amoeba_proteus_with_many_pseudopodia.jpg">SmallRex/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>

<h2>Discovering life at a new extreme</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/eukaryote">Eukaryotic cells</a>, like the ones found in our bodies, contain <a href="https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Organelle">organelles</a> like <a href="https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Nucleus">nuclei</a> and <a href="https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Mitochondria">mitochondria</a>. Eukaryotic organisms are reported less often than bacteria in extreme conditions, and based on observations from fungi at 140 F (60 C), scientists had theorized that eukaryotic <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.69.9.2426">life is not physically possible</a> beyond 143 F (62 C). </p>

<p>In our new study, our team <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.08.043">isolated and characterized a unicellular eukaryote</a>, <em>Incendiamoeba cascadensis</em>, which is able to reproduce at 145 F (63 C). This finding marks the highest temperature yet recorded for eukaryotic life.</p>

<p>Our team found <em>Incendiamoeba cascadensis</em> in geothermal springs in <a href="https://www.nationalparks.org/explore/parks/lassen-volcanic-national-park">Lassen Volcanic National Park</a>, in Northern California, but we suspect it might also be found in other geothermal areas worldwide. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Two authors of the study, Angela Oliverio and Beryl Rappaport, at geothermal springs in Lassen Volcanic National Park in Northern California.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">A.M. Oliverio</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://www.livescience.com/54281-amoeba-definition.html">Like many amoebae</a> – cells that change shape as they move – <em>Incendiamoeba</em> is a forager. It can move around in search of food and favorable conditions. It actively crawls at 147 F (64 C), but a few degrees more and it will enter a protective hibernation-like state.</p>

<h2>What sets thermophiles apart?</h2>

<p>While bacteria have been recorded <a href="https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.68.4.1735-1742.2002">living up to</a> 212 F (100 C), it is unclear why eukaryotic cells are less amenable to high temperatures and other extremes. Many theories abound: Our cells have more protective membranes, including several membranes within each cell, surrounding their organelles. We also have complex molecular machinery that maintains our large genomes, and a <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/cytoskeleton">dynamic cytoskeleton</a>: a network of proteins that allows our cells to move.</p>

<p>Like other eukaryotes, <em>Incendiamoeba</em> has organelles, an active cytoskeleton and a relatively large genome, so what allows it to persist where others cannot? So far, <em>Incendiamoeba</em> has revealed that we don’t yet know which parts of eukaryotes are generally incompatible with high temperature. </p>

<p>As someone who investigates phenomena at the molecular level, I am always thinking about how molecules move and how motion increases with temperature. At higher temperatures, the velcrolike bonds holding proteins together can unfold, preventing them from performing their vital functions. Eukaryotes have evolved protein helpers called <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/biochemistry-genetics-and-molecular-biology/heat-shock-protein">heat shock proteins</a>, which detect protein unfolding and help refold them. </p>

<p>So, could <em>Incendiamoeba</em> simply have more of these helper proteins? Our team found that it does have a large reservoir of heat shock proteins, but making these proteins requires a lot of energy, and they must be folded themselves, so more helper proteins probably isn’t the full answer. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><em>Incendiamoeba</em> also has a unique set of protein building blocks that are good at holding proteins together. Yet this composition may only make up for the fact that proteins degrade more easily with increasing temperature. </p>

<p>We can look at <em>Incendiamoeba’s</em> genes, which turn on – or up – when temperature rises. Many of these genes are unknown. It is possible that one of these mystery genes is the key to its ability to withstand high temperatures. However, it is more likely, and in my mind, much more interesting, that there exists a symphony of small changes this organism has evolved, which confer its unique abilities. </p>

<p>By investigating <em>Incendiamoeba</em> and finding others like it, we can determine those changes and learn about the key principles for how life works on our environmentally diverse planet.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293407/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road

<title>Driverless 18-wheelers are on a few highways, but widespread use is a long way down the road</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766851/original/file-20261017-50-su17bt.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C4229%2C2819&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A self-driving tractor-trailer cruises around a test track in Pittsburgh.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Self%20Driving%20Trucks/b534c0f31cee4e639c5f31e829971b81/photo">AP/Gene J. Puskar</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping. A few companies have begun testing early models on some limited routes <a href="https://selfdrivenews.com/international-and-ryder-trial-l4-autonomous-trucks/">in Texas</a> <a href="https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/14/self-driving-trucks-are-officially-testing-on-california-highways/">and California</a>. Simulations of automated fleets show the potential benefits of the technology: The vehicles could improve safety, enhance fuel economy and lessen transit times. </p>

<p>Truck makers and operators still have to solve some major issues, however, including how automated trucks will operate in variable weather and road conditions, and whether drivers should still be inside big rigs. </p>

<p>I am <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=AQcftaEAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">an engineer</a> who <a href="https://www.umass.edu/engineering/about/directory/shannon-roberts">studies human factors and transportation safety</a>, and in my view, it is likely that automated trucks and human drivers will be working together for quite some time. </p>

<h2>Benefits of automation</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.sae.org/standards/j3016_202104-taxonomy-definitions-terms-related-driving-automation-systems-road-motor-vehicles">Fully automated trucks</a>, which can drive on an interstate highway in good weather without human intervention, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trip.2026.102309">use a combination</a> of AI, machine learning, computer vision, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. <a href="https://torc.ai/data-loop-simulation-autonomous-trucks-development/">Torc</a>, one company developing these vehicles, uses AI to combine data from multiple sensors and generate models that predict truck performance.</p>

<p>Data taken from modern big rigs that are equipped with certain technology such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/15389588.2021.1893700">automatic emergency braking</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aap.2010.10.033">lane-keeping assistance systems</a> indicate that fully automated, driverless trucks could reduce the number and severity of crashes. They could also save fuel and therefore cost by <a href="https://www.transportation.gov/av/workforce/report">optimizing acceleration and braking</a>, and by running multiple vehicles in a close-knit <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trb.2017.10.016">convoy or platoon</a>. Driverless trucks could <a href="https://doi.org/10.1061/9780784483138.004">reduce parking needs as well as emissions from idling</a> because they could run almost 24 hours a day and would not need to idle when they do park, which is common for regular rigs at truck stops.</p>

<p>Finally, automated trucks could help ease the ongoing <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tranpol.2025.103907">driver shortage</a>. Ironically, automation could make driving less stressful and less physically demanding, <a href="https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-19-161">improving job satisfaction among drivers</a>.</p>

<h2>Weather and work zones are hard to navigate</h2>

<p>The main reason automated trucks are not common today is that they have difficulty operating in variable weather, under changing roadway conditions and alongside unpredictable drivers. </p>

<p>Automated trucks require sensors, radars and cameras that gather information about the environment around them to make decisions. However, snow and rain remain a problem <a href="https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/bams/101/11/bamsD190035.xml">for all automated vehicles</a>, including cars, because they prevent the technology from “seeing” the roadway. Driverless taxi company Waymo, for example, only operates driverless cars in areas that get no snow.</p>

<p>Furthermore, any stretch of road where there may not be a predictable, clear surface and prevalent lines <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/OJVT.2023.3335180">is difficult to handle</a>. Imagine a construction zone with orange cones, narrow lanes and missing lane lines. Driverless car companies still try to <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/18/waymo-nhtsa-voluntary-recall-robotaxis-entered-freeway-construction-zones.html">avoid these areas</a>. And, oddly, some research shows that automobile drivers tend to crash into driverless cars <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-48526-4">at a higher rate</a> than they do cars piloted by people.</p>

<p>Given those challenges, companies are testing automated trucks on roads that lack complications. </p>

<p>For example, autonomous truck maker Aurora is <a href="https://ir.aurora.tech/news-events/press-releases/detail/119/aurora-begins-commercial-driverless-trucking-in-texas-ushering-in-a-new-era-of-freight">operating large freight trucks on I-45</a>, a relatively flat and straight highway between Dallas and Houston. Rival Kodiak’s robotrucks are <a href="https://ir.atlas.energy/news-events/press-releases/detail/47/kodiak-delivers-customer-owned-autonomous-robotrucks-to">delivering sand to industrial sites</a> in Texas over roads few people use. Few if any automated trucks are being tested in chaotic urban environments, given the pedestrians, bicyclists, traffic lights and elements of city traffic.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Y0jUMEzjLb4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Driverless trucks are operating on some roads in Texas.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some companies that were developing automated trucks have scaled back ambitions, changed direction or exited the market. </p>

<p>In 2023, Embark, TuSimple and Locomotion <a href="https://liveinthefuture.org/stories/autonomous-trucking-graveyard">closed down</a>. Waymo began to <a href="https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2023/07/waymo-kills-off-autonomous-trucking-program/">focus solely on cars</a>. Other companies narrowed their focus to trucks that would operate only along a <a href="https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/technology/2025/05/12/521130/two-companies-begin-testing-driverless-commercial-trucks-in-houston-area/">few dedicated routes between two large cities</a> or manufacturing sites.</p>

<h2>Drivers and trucks that work together</h2>

<p>In my view, for years to come, automated trucks with AI-based controls will still require a driver. </p>

<p>The best technology will support a symbiosis between human and machine, where the person and the truck each do what they do best. A human would likely drive the truck across the “first mile” – the uncertain and crowded warehouse grounds and local streets to a highway. The driver would then stop using the steering wheel, gas pedal and brake and let automation take over. The human would take back control during the “last mile” to the truck’s final destination.</p>

<p>Research my colleagues and I conducted shows that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trf.2026.103758">human-machine interfaces</a> that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trf.2024.08.014">communicate between drivers and autonomous vehicles</a> will be key. For example, a screen or heads-up display inside the cab would tell the driver how the technology is doing. Verbal messages or a vibrating seat could signal that the automation cannot handle a developing situation, and the driver would take over. </p>

<p>Developers will have to be aware of possible biases. So-called <a href="https://doi.org/10.1108/ICS-08-2025-0318">automation bias</a> could lead to a driver who trusts and relies on the truck’s decision-making so much that they defer to it. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/0960085X.2021.1927212">Algorithmic bias</a> could cause truck sensors to recognize certain groups of people on the road more than others, such as only detecting pedestrians of a certain size or shape.</p>

<p>The long-term vision is to have no driver, in part to lower costs. But driverless trucks do not seem to me to be practical on a large scale in the near future. It is more realistic to envision the driver and the automated truck as a team. Vehicle manufacturers, technology developers, regulators and drivers will need to work together to realize the benefits.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291123/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

She has previously received funding from Belron, GM, and Toyota Collaborative Safety Research Center.</span></em></p></content>

title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news

<title>Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768941/original/file-20261028-52-sa4d3n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2015%2C1344&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Some local papers that were on the verge of extinction, like the Solon Economist in Iowa, have teamed up with universities as a way to get staffing and support.</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Photo from Teri Finneman</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the <a href="https://soloneconomist.com/">Solon Economist</a> was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024. </p>

<p>But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa.</p>

<p>It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “<a href="https://www.cislm.org/what-exactly-is-a-news-desert/">news desert</a>” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets.</p>

<p>These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site <a href="https://noticieromovil.com/">Noticiero Móvil</a> at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/@GoodMorningIndianCountry">Good Morning Indian Country</a>” at the University of Kansas, to <a href="https://thescopeboston.org/">The Scope at Northeastern</a> in Boston. </p>

<p>We’re <a href="https://journalism.ku.edu/people/teri-finneman-phd">journalism professors</a> <a href="https://www.duq.edu/faculty-and-staff/pamela-walck.php">who have studied and experienced the opportunities</a> and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “<a href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/news-desert-u-9781978765047/">News Desert U</a>,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis.</p>

<h2>Knowing your community</h2>

<p>These experiments come against a grim backdrop. </p>

<p>Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to <a href="https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/">Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report</a>. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s <a href="https://localnewsinitiative.northwestern.edu/projects/state-of-local-news/2025/report/">2025 report estimated</a> that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years.</p>

<p>But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/7FZ7mPdN9vQ?wmode=transparent&amp;start=3" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How the University of Iowa stepped in to save the Solon Economist.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work.</p>

<p>Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently. </p>

<p>In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers.</p>

<p>The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff. </p>

<p>“They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.”</p>

<p>Student Publications <a href="https://www.uvm.edu/ccn/news/iowa-student-newspaper-acquires-two-local-outlets">bought both newspapers</a> for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships. </p>

<p>Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.” </p>

<p>“People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.”</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Chris Umscheid, editor of the Solon Economist in Iowa, stands next to a newspaper rack with print editions." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/768048/original/file-20261023-50-w532dc.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Teri Finneman</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger.</p>

<p>Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000.</p>

<p>Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.”</p>

<h2>A $10 deal</h2>

<p>Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the <a href="https://www.theoglethorpeecho.com/">The Oglethorpe Echo</a>.</p>

<p>Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/A5rskhYV_Zk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=11" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How the Oglethorpe Echo found a new owner.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>“I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.” </p>

<p>NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership.  </p>

<p>In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added.</p>

<p>The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed. </p>

<p>Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county. </p>

<p>The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds. </p>

<p>She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit.</p>

<p>When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester. </p>

              <span class="caption">Amanda Bright’s journalism students at The University of Georgia rotate across different roles to develop writing, editing and multimedia skills.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Teri Finneman</span>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said.</p>

<p>But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat.</p>

<p>But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said.</p>

<p>Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added.</p>

<h2>Service over profits</h2>

<p>One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships. </p>

<p>The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances. </p>

<p>These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting. </p>

<p>Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view.</p>

<p>“Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.”</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292102/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture
And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa
It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “ news desert ” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades
And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets

These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “ Good Morning Indian Country ” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston
We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education
Our new book, “ News Desert U ,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news
We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis

Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers
Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years

title: The case for a little election optimism
excerpt: President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 27, 2026. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This sto
body: President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 27, 2026. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

No sooner had early voting started this year than analysts noticed a curious trend: Democratic voters were choosing to vote a lot like…Republicans.  Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Democrats who cast their ballots early have most commonly done so by mail
But this year, they’re voting in person , and in huge numbers — even narrowing Republicans’ traditional early voting lead in states like Florida and Texas

The abrupt shift may have something to do with President Donald Trump’s attempts to undermine the mail voting process , and it almost definitely reflects the anxiety and vigilance that many Americans feel about the midterms this year

In less than a week, they’ll decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices.  The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits

So as we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’ve been partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for a series of weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms.  Previously, we dug into the ways both parties are changing , the bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers , the politics of high costs, and the changing mood toward Israel
This week, for our final installment, we’re tackling something a little more fundamental: the integrity and security of the voting process itself
It’s a worrying subject, but by no means a hopeless one
Go a little deeper Let me begin with a metaphor that may or may not reassure you: Imagine there’s a serial killer outside your house, and they’re trying to get in and kill you
That’s pretty terrifying, under any circumstance
But also: Your house is an absolute vault

And the police are actually on its way now. “I don’t want to understate the threat” of election interference, Benjy Sarlin, Vox’s editorial director of politics said when he relayed this metaphor  on the America, Actually podcast last month
But if Trump is the serial killer trying America’s doors and windows…then understand this house is pretty well-defended.  Take mail voting, the issue that has so (literally) moved Democrats this year

You’ll recall that Trump tried to sabotage the practice by implementing new, last-minute rules that would have effectively canceled mail-in voting in some places.  But the Constitution clearly assigns the power to regulate and administer elections to the states and Congress, and courts blocked the administration’s rules
In mid-September, the Supreme Court declined to let them take effect for this election
So there’s one lock made good.  The Trump administration has also demanded unprecedented access to states’ voter rolls, suing 30 states and Washington, DC, to obtain them
Of those cases, courts have dismissed 27 of them (though many dismissals are being appealed)
Earlier this month, the DOJ went further and demanded that California officials  set aside the ballots of some 20,000 registered voters that it alleged were likely noncitizens
In the predictable legal battle that followed, courts sided with the state

A federal judge excoriated the administration in an opinion on Wednesday , ruling that the ballot segregation order “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election.” The Trump administration has already appealed the ruling.  Other forms of meddling are possible

Asked in August about declaring a national emergency to impose new voting requirements, Trump replied — unnervingly — that “stranger things have happened.” And the president and his allies have floated drastic measures like deploying federal agents to polling sites or seizing “suspect” ballots, a threat tangible enough that it’s reportedly unsettled a number of FBI agents.  Just last week, the Trump administration attempted to preemptively contest the results in Alaska’s Senate race, claiming that the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot — the incumbent Republican and an independent newcomer — risked confusing voters
The New York Times has since reported that Democrats enticed Dan Sullivan 2.0 to run for exactly that reason
In some corners, the ensuing scandal has raised concerns that Republicans could refuse to seat Democrat Mary Peltola if she wins.  But even that possibility is fairly remote
While there are mechanisms for both state officials and US lawmakers to challenge election results, those procedures are pretty regimented

And any attempts to disrupt voting, vote-counting, or the certification of results would likely face both a flood of lawsuits (which voting groups have already prepped ) and a public outcry that could ultimately and lastingly hurt Republicans
Trump might not care overmuch about democratic norms or the rule of law, but he does likely care about the risks of a longer-term political backlash

To this day, Benjy said, a lot of Republicans still blame Trump for losing them Georgia’s Senate seats: His election denialism after 2020 helped drive huge numbers of Black Georgians to the polls, where they voted in two Democrats.  The number of Democrats voting early and in-person suggests the possibility that a similar dynamic is at play now

In other words, there is real risk — but lots of people are fighting to keep the proverbial bad guys out.  Races to watch: Alaska Senate race, where Trump is ready to contest a Democratic win ; Wisconsin governor’s race, where  Republican Tom Tiffany has promoted Trump’s lies about the 2020 election;  Nevada’s secretary of state race, which could similarly put an outspoken election denier in charge of the state’s voting system
More from Vox:  How election officials are thinking about Trump’s threat to the midterms The one thing everyone can do to fight for free and fair elections Trump has a plan to steal the midterms
One link for later ➨ Turn on the (early morning) lights
It’s getting darker earlier and earlier these days, and it’s often pitch black when my alarm goes off
That means it’s time for an annual tradition: digging out my bulky, 10,000-lux light box
Bright morning light, from a box or the sun, sets your body’s internal clock and helps regulate your sleep

It can also mitigate seasonal affective disorder, which starts plaguing many sufferers around Halloween.   Before you go… Did you know… that there’s an extremely rare and spooky form of lightning that can appear indoors? It’s called “ball lightning,” and it’s one of the most mysterious weather phenomena in the world.   Today’s trivia: What’s the name of the vast Andean empire that ruled from its capital in Cusco? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you where you might find an arroyo
These seasonally dry streambeds cut through deserts, where they can serve as a “highway” for wild animals.

title: Democrats have big healthcare plans. The industry is preparing for a fight.
excerpt: Protesters in Minnesota advocate for universal healthcare. | David Berding/Getty Images for People's Action Institute Americans want changes to their healthcare
body: Protesters in Minnesota advocate for universal healthcare. | David Berding/Getty Images for People's Action Institute Americans want changes to their healthcare, and the candidates in this year’s midterms are making bold promises about how they are going to improve it: Medicare-for-all , or a public health insurance option , or free primary care for everyone

If Democrats win big this year, they could build up momentum to control Congress and the White House in 2029, which could leave them well-positioned to take on the thorny problem of how to fix the US health system
For every Affordable Care Act, you have the failed attempt to repeal it or the calamity of the Clinton-era healthcare initiative
Americans want change — but they fear it, too
I’ve spent years reading healthcare polls , talking to voters , attending focus groups
The public’s opinion of the healthcare industry has grown more and more sour, and distrust of the medical establishment is at an all-time high

People are sick of having a broken health system, but they worry that big changes could end up being bad for them.  Even though a meaningful attempt at reform is still years away and universal health care in any form might seem like a progressive pipe dream, the industry is not sitting idly by.  As Democrats have started to roll out policy proposals in anticipation of winning back Congress, the industry has been there to start making its case

In some campaigns, that means backing Republicans, but it also means lobbying Democratic Party leaders to hold the line against their more progressive members who want to push for far-reaching changes.  The question now is: Will their old playbook work? Can the industry convince Democrats to scale back their policy ambitions, or is their grip on Congress loosening? “The next two years are actually quite pivotal, for doing the groundwork and all the necessary socializing, consensus-building,” said Kim Monk , a former congressional healthcare staffer who co-founded the private-sector research firm Capital Alpha Partners. “That’s the work that gets you to a point where either party decides, okay, this will be on our platform — or not.” That will be the tug-of-war of the next two years: a PR battle waged between health companies with hundreds of millions of dollars at their disposal on one side and progressive lawmakers, activists, and patient advocates on the other that will ultimately determine what’s possible in the next phase of American healthcare

The healthcare industry doesn’t want Democrats to win too big In the short term, the industry is hedging its bets in the face of a Democratic wave.  Private enterprise has historically backed the Republican Party, but that’s starting to shift
What the healthcare industry values above all else is balance
Democrats operating without any constraints are more likely to impose government regulations on medical companies

But full GOP control comes with its own risks, like the $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts passed as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which has already led to clinics and hospitals laying off staff or even closing facilities altogether
Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems

How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy

Sign up here . “At least for the short term, I imagine the healthcare industry would welcome control of Congress by Democrats, creating more predictability, forestalling more cuts in Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act, and potentially reversing or delaying some of the cuts that have already been made,” said Larry Levitt , executive vice president for health policy at KFF. “The longer-term political calculus for the healthcare industry is more complicated

Many Democrats are pushing for a bigger role for government in health care.” In other words, while healthcare companies might welcome a Democratic House as a check on President Donald Trump’s unpredictability, they aren’t necessarily hoping for a massive blue wave that could make significant reforms a serious possibility if Democrats were to win the White House in 2028.  The industry’s MO when it looks like a wave election is brewing is to balance the scales: I reported in 2016 how, in what was looking like a good year for Democrats, the drug industry poured money into the campaigns of Republican candidates by a 6-to-1 margin in competitive races, hoping to stifle the agenda of presumed President Hillary Clinton. (Of course they, like the rest of us, are still susceptible to being wrong.) And that’s how the industry has been approaching the 2026 election: In many of the pivotal House and Senate races, they are backing the GOP.  As healthcare journalist Merrill Goozner reported last week, the American Hospital Association PAC and PhRMA, a drug industry trade group, have given a combined $14,500 to Republican incumbent Jon Husted and none to his Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown in the historically expensive Ohio Senate race

Susan Collins has received donations from all of the major healthcare trade groups — hospitals, pharma, insurers, and doctors — while her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, got none. (He also has sworn off corporate PAC money.) Even in an open race without an incumbent, like the Iowa Senate campaign, the Republican candidate has scored donations from hospitals and pharma, but the Democrat has not, Goozner reported

If Democrats take the House but not the Senate, that would immediately put a damper on their healthcare reform plans — whereas winning a Senate majority would allow them to start drafting and debating bills in both chambers with an eye toward what could actually pass if they win in 2028 too. “If there is actually a blue tsunami next week and Democrats get 51-plus [members] in the Senate, that’s a really big deal,” Monk said. “You can’t just say this doesn’t matter because Trump’s going to veto it, because I think it very much becomes a 2028 issue.” And even as they work to push the next Congress more to their ideological liking, the healthcare industry is preparing for the fight that comes after
The industry is prepping its counterattacks on ambitious healthcare proposals After the midterms wrap up, the next two years in Congress and on the presidential campaign trail will be crucial
The industry is already working to set the terms of the debate and push back against big changes

Each subset of the industry has its own versions of this argument: Pharma warns that price controls could stifle innovation , insurers warn that coverage mandates will increase premiums, hospitals warn that constraints on their funding could lead to closures and job losses. (There’s a well-known saying among DC insiders that every congressional district has a hospital , making every member potentially susceptible to the industry’s message that new healthcare legislation could result in their own constituents losing their jobs.) They’ve started by trying to discredit the more sweeping health policy proposals before new members ever arrive in Washington, DC

In Texas, for instance, Republican groups have leaned on an industry-commissioned study to attack Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico for supporting Medicare-for-all, warning that it would lead to cuts for rural hospitals — at least according to an analysis produced by the Partnership for America’s Future, a coalition of industry groups that exists explicitly to oppose Medicare-for-all or a public option
They ran a similar ad against Democrat Janelle Stelson, who’s trying to topple incumbent Rep

Scott Perry in Pennsylvania.  The industry is trying to plant the idea in voters’ minds that these big, bold proposals may sound superficially appealing, but carry significant risks: You could lose your plan, you could lose your doctor, you could pay higher taxes. (And they often have their own studies to back those arguments, like the one cited in this year’s campaign, to counter the evidence offered by advocates in support of reform.) And it might work exactly like it has in the past

As John McDonough, a former congressional healthcare staffer and author of America’s Wrong Turn: US Health Care in the Neoliberal Era , put it to me, the history is clear: “Every comprehensive effort, defeat, and every incremental effort succeeds.” That is in part because of the healthcare industry’s influence and its success in framing the debate
On top of trying to sway the competitive races, the industry is also trying to keep its most important allies within both parties happy ahead of the midterms

As the Center for Health and Democracy’s data shows , the health insurance industry PACs alone have given tens of thousands of dollars to Democratic and Republican leaders, as well as senior members of the healthcare-focused House and Senate committees
It’s another hedge, an attempt to keep the members who will decide what’s on the agenda next year on their side
The industry supports reversing the GOP’s massive Medicaid cuts and increasing funding for the ACA marketplaces, two top-priority items for Democrats if they win Congress in the midterms
But they are hoping the party’s leaders will steer their members away from some of their more radical ideas for overhauling healthcare

Because while individual sectors within healthcare may squabble over smaller-scale reforms, the entire industry is united against plans to fundamentally change the US health system. (They are also increasingly owned by the same parent company, as consolidation in the medical sector becomes more and more common.) “The healthcare industry is all for more people having coverage and stable government financing,” Levitt said, “but will circle the wagons to fight Medicare-for-all.” Already, whenever Democrats start talking about their health policy ideas, the industry is ready with a response

Last month, as some Democrats announced support for a public insurance option, the Partnership for America’s Health Care Future argued it would reduce access. “A public option is not the answer to the affordability and access challenges patients and families are facing,” said the group’s executive director, Lauren Crawford Shaver

Meanwhile, the health insurance lobbying group, AHIP, released a 40-page document in October on how to improve affordability and access, using it in part to argue against a public option because it would “stifle competition and threaten the coverage most Americans want to keep.” Centrist Democratic groups who receive industry support have said they are “preparing for war” against Medicare-for-all, according to the news outlet Sludge
The industry is not omnipotent, however, and the debate could still change if Americans’ healthcare gets worse over the next few years
The US uninsured rate has been on the rise as pandemic protections expire and the costs of healthcare rise for millions

Unless Democrats succeed in stopping the Republican Medicaid and ACA cuts in the OBBBA, that problem is going to get worse — and that could also force Democrats to think bigger about how to fix it. “I am not sure anyone has fully absorbed how damaging and disruptive that is going to be — including to hospitals and health systems,” Jonathan Oberlander , professor of social medicine at the University of North Carolina and the former editor of the Journal of Health Politics, Policy and Law , told me over email. “Large coverage losses will trigger great instability in health politics and perhaps open more of a window to bolder proposals.” So, will the industry’s arguments still have juice? After the medical industry enjoyed a brief rebound in popularity during the pandemic, 50 percent of Americans say they have a negative view of it, while 37 percent have a positive view, per Gallup

And the appetite for reform is growing: 64 percent of Americans say it is the government’s responsibility to make sure that everyone has healthcare coverage — the highest share at any time, except for the late 2000s, shortly before the ACA became law

Even the hospital industry, which has long enjoyed more public support than pharma or insurance companies, is seeing its popularity waver: A Families USA poll from August found that an overwhelming 81 percent of Americans thought hospital prices were unreasonable. “Hospitals have done a great job of pleading poverty on Capitol Hill. ‘We’re probably the only provider who basically has to provide care to whoever shows up
Just give us more money,’” Monk said. “I think that argument is wearing a little bit thin.”
