title: How to come up with a last-minute Halloween costume without spending a ton of money
excerpt: Editor’s note, October 29, 2026, 10:15 am ET: This article was originally published in 2022 and has been updated for Halloween 2026
body: Editor’s note, October 29, 2026, 10:15 am ET: This article was originally published in 2022 and has been updated for Halloween 2026
With an October 30 birthday, it’s only natural that Kimberly Murphy takes Halloween extremely seriously

A natural redhead, Murphy has dressed up as iconic crimson-haired characters like the Wendy’s mascot and Chuckie from Rugrats , but once she started dating her now-fiancé, Brian, nearly a decade ago, Murphy’s costumes leveled up
A selection of Murphy and Brian’s greatest Halloween hits: Dexter and Dee Dee from Dexter’s Laboratory, Ms

Frizzle and the eponymous bus from The Magic School Bus , Jack and Sally from The Nightmare Before Christmas, Tormund and Brienne of Tarth from Game of Thrones , and Shaun White and a snowboard.  “We put my snowboard on his back so I could actually ‘ride’ him,” Murphy, who, regardless of the character’s gender, always dresses as the redhead, says. “It gave a funny, experiential element to the costume.” This October, the couple, both in their early 30s, is getting married and will be depicting Chucky and Bride of Chucky for Halloween. (You can guess who’ll be donning the white dress.) In childhood, Halloween is one of the few days of the year when you can wear your most imaginative garb to school and to strangers’ doors
As you get older, that sense of youthful creativity might wane, and figuring out what to wear to a costume party becomes another minor conundrum
Whether you dabble in dress-up or are a cosplay aficionado, conceiving of creative, yet approachable, Halloween attire doesn’t need to be a bewildering or expensive experience
Experts in the art of costuming offer their advice for ideating and executing your best guise so you can take home top honors in this year’s costume contest
Narrow your focus When every character, celebrity, historical figure, animal, pun, and meme is potential costume fodder, homing in on one idea can feel overwhelming
Limitations and parameters are your best friend
Use your own appearance — is there a person or fictional character who has a similar style as you? Vaguely comparable features? — and the media that interested you this year as jumping-off points

Everything from YA novels and nostalgic ‘90s TV shows to extremely local jokes and gags ( public transit , sports mascots ) to niche memes (hello, Chris Pine astral projecting ) are prime inspo.  Is there an alter ego you’re interested in exploring? Cosplayer and photographer Hope Elmekies often dresses up as characters she feels a personal connection to, like Morticia Addams. “I very much felt like I related to [her] because she’s not fitting in,” she says. “I felt that kinship to that character.” For all of her costumes, Murphy has let her red hair and the height difference between her and her fiancé (she’s 5 feet tall, he’s 6-foot-2) guide her choices
She thinks back to significant pop culture or historical moments that fall under these categories

For example, Murphy flagged Queen’s Gambit as a potential ensemble, due to its buzzworthiness and the fact that the protagonist had red hair. “I take this formulaic approach to Halloween where if it’s unusually small or redheaded,” she says, “that fits my formula of a potential Halloween candidate.” For group or family costumes, it can be helpful to focus on one shared interest, accessory, or hobby
If you all met in an adult dodgeball league, maybe you want to dress up as dodgeball players
Maybe your group is composed of three couples and you want to do a Grease -inspired collab
Then, figure out what effect you’d like your costume to have
Is your goal to make everyone laugh? Be the sexy one? Go all-in on minute details? Incorporate a few friends for a group costume? This can help you zero in on an idea
The location of your Halloween bash can help further narrow down your options, says custom costume maker Correen Borst-Straub of Correen’s Creative Designs
Think about where you’ll wear the getup to determine what’s appropriate

If you’re going to a party in a small apartment, you probably won’t want to wear a huge Marie Antoinette dress, or you might want to think twice about wearing vampire fangs to a costumed fundraiser with a sit-down dinner
Buck convention, respectfully Using popular culture as inspiration may yield a few potential ideas, but if you really want a memorable guise, approach these concepts in an unconventional manner
Many people tend to dress up as the main characters from popular shows, but supporting roles or genre tropes can also be crowd-pleasing attire

For her all-time favorite Halloween costume, Dani Cabot, the manager of New York City vintage boutique Screaming Mimis , dressed up as a virgin sacrifice. “I got bedsheets and a classic cheesy ’70s Roman goddess dress and I got a huge wig, and then a choker that made it look like my throat was slashed,” she says
Even if you don’t share every physical trait with a character, use your differences to your advantage

Murphy and her fiancé have often dressed up as characters that have historically been depicted as opposite to the couple’s own gender presentation. “Gender is always very subjective,” says Philadelphia-based drag queen VinChelle . “Everyone can express themselves how they want to.” VinChelle frequently performs in looks inspired by Beyoncé and uses the star’s photoshoots as a reference

She’ll then scour fabric stores in Philadelphia or New York City for the garment and works closely with seamstresses to construct the outfit. “Beyoncé’s a glorified drag queen,” she says.   View this post on Instagram To be clear: This is not an excuse to appropriate other cultures , use makeup to darken your skin, or wear racist costumes

If you’re unsure if a costume is appropriate, run your idea by a few friends first, says Kate Farrier, the wardrobe manager for RWS Entertainment Group , an entertainment and event production company that has produced haunted experiences for the likes of Six Flags Great America, Sea World, and Legoland
Reference your personal style Think about ways you can infuse your personality into popular ideas

What can you do to make the costume feel like you? If your one wardrobe staple is a leather jacket, make your witch persona wear a leather jacket. “If you’re always on your phone, maybe you’re a celebrity vampire, social media vampire,” Farrier says. “Try and make it about something that you always have by bringing your personal items into it because that will make it special for you.” One year, a shopper at Screaming Mimis spiced up their vampire attire by adding ’70s disco accessories. “They did this insane disco Studio 54 vampire look,” Cabot says

You can also take a character who isn’t particularly known for their fashion, like Pac-Man , and make an interesting garment inspired by their aesthetic.  Another way to differentiate is to make subtle changes to tried-and-true depictions
Borst-Straub has a 25 percent rule; she infuses her creativity into well-known designs so the resulting look is 75 percent true to pop culture and 25 percent her own
Elmekies gets inspiration by searching her costume idea plus “cosplay” on Pinterest to see how others have approached the concept

Don’t worry about being so niche that everyone has to ask you what you are, Elmekies says. “So, what are you?” is a great icebreaker. “Sometimes when I go out as Belle from Beauty and the Beast , people don’t know who I am necessarily because it’s not a Disney knockoff; it’s more built that you can wear every day,” Elmekies says.  Use what you’ve got (or shop secondhand) Halloween outfits shouldn’t cost a ton of money
Think about the colors, shapes, and silhouettes needed for a costume to help you identify the look’s building blocks

For a gargoyle look, for example, you’ll need a lot of gray apparel and makeup. “Think about the shapes of things instead of the actual items,” says Ryan Walton, the producer of Halloween experiences for RWS Entertainment Group. “[Say] I need a round hoop-like thing
What can I do that’s round and hoop-like that’s not going to cost me a lot of money and then I can refabricate?” Scour your closet (or your friends’ closets) for pieces you’ll need
If you’re dressing up as a flapper, dig out a slip dress if you have one

Then, let your accessories and props do all the talking. “So things like jewelry, gloves, stockings, headpieces, masks can really transform a basic into something that’s excellent,” Cabot says.  For any pieces you don’t already own, visit a local vintage or thrift store or indie costume shop to get materials
Workers at these stores can offer expert costuming advice, and by shopping in person, you can be sure you’re getting exactly what you want — no online ordering surprises, Cabot says

title: The fix for America’s terrible internet is hiding in Tennessee
excerpt: Chattanooga’s publicly owned internet network has helped transform the once struggling city into an unlikely marvel of civic reinvention. | Lucy Jones for Vox;
body: Chattanooga’s publicly owned internet network has helped transform the once struggling city into an unlikely marvel of civic reinvention. | Lucy Jones for Vox; Getty Images Most Americans hate their cable companies

But not the 200,000-odd residents of Chattanooga, Tennessee, a city nestled in the Appalachian foothills.  For many people, the city might seem off the beaten path — enough so that when Spain’s national team chose the city as their base during the FIFA World Cup over the summer, the internet exploded with jeers of incredulity

And yet, as many an urban planner, and certainly many a local, will tell you, Chattanooga is a special place, known not just because the Glenn Miller Orchestra immortalized it as a scenic hub for the choo-choo train

No, what really has put Chattanooga on the map recently is its ridiculously fast, municipally owned internet.  Key takeaways Chattanooga, Tennessee, is home to some of the fastest, most beloved broadband in the nation
It’s all thanks to the city’s publicly owned internet network, which has been linked to billions of dollars in economic benefits since coming online in 2010
Hundreds of other cities have followed suit in the years since, but many others have been stymied by opposition from major cable companies
And that’s a shame, because if every city was like Chattanooga, our internet could be so much better than it is now
Unlike almost everywhere else in the country, the fiber-optic cables that keep much of Chattanooga online were laid neither by Comcast nor Spectrum, but by the city itself

In a $220 million gamble, its public power utility, EPB, has helped transform the once struggling post-industrial city into an unlikely marvel of civic reinvention , and an inspiration for many other dozens of copycat towns around the country.   When it debuted in 2010 , at one gigabit per second, the city’s ultra-speedy broadband was among the fastest in the world , as fast as global meccas like Hong Kong, and over 200 times faster than the average top-tier offering across the US. “This makes Chattanooga, a mid-sized city in the South,” declared then-Mayor Ron Littlefield to the New York Times , “one of the leading cities in the world in its digital capabilities.”  In the decade and a half since Chattanooga rebranded as “Gig City,” its trademark broadband has proved to be far more than a mere fancy gimmick

It has added billions of dollars to the city’s economy, lured in hundreds of new startups, and, according to EPB, become the single largest source of funding for local public schools, and delighted hundreds of thousands of local customers.  If you’re not a tech company or a prolific streamer, of course, you may not need such intensive internet service

But the city’s broadband service is widely beloved locally for bringing 70 percent of households online at, by far, the lowest price per megabit of bandwidth in the area and quite possibly, among the lowest in the country

Consumer Reports perennially ranks EPB among America’s best providers, a sentiment apparently shared by the legions of Chattanoogans who take to social media to sing EPB’s praises every time it swoops in to fix an outage minutes after a storm hits, or bemoan their loss when they move away and witness the sludgy pace at — and high rates — which the rest of us browse and scroll.  “Chattanooga turned out better than anyone could have hoped,” said Christopher Mitchell, director of the Community Broadband Networks Initiative, part of the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, a group that researches locally owned infrastructure, “and the one thing that hasn’t changed are their prices

It’s rare, remarkable even.” That original single-gig service runs $68 per month, and faster speeds aren’t too much more.   But even as the benefits of Chattanooga’s internet supremacy have compounded, public broadband networks like it are still a rarity across the US , which you probably already know if you, like most Americans, have ever sensed your internet growing ever more lethargic , even as your fees climb month after month.  There is a better way, and Chattanooga has long since shown the nation how

For better or worse , the internet drives much of our daily lives and the economy, and what makes the internet possible? Broadband, which is powered by those stiff plastic-sheathed cables filled with strands of thin glass or braids of copper wire, beaming pulses of light or electricity into your modem

And yet, the US has outsourced the provision of this precious public good almost entirely to de facto monopolies that keep our internet slower, more expensive, and above all, more infuriating than it needs to be.  “There was a generation that built water systems and electric systems
There was a generation that built the roads,” Mitchell said

Today, however, “People are just afraid of the idea of the government being ambitious and doing what Chattanooga did.” How Chattanooga built the world’s best broadband Long before Chattanooga grew famous for its broadband, it was known, for a period of time, as “the dirtiest city of America,” a moniker bestowed by Walter Cronkite in 1969.  According to local lore, the moon pie, which originated at a bakery in Chattanooga, came to be when a coal miner asked for a snack “ as big as the moon ” to sustain him for long shifts down the shaft

The coal he mined fueled the industrial boom that defined Chattanooga until the mid-20th century, when the city’s factories, furnaces, and railroads belched a smog so noxious, it melted women’s nylon stockings off their legs as they walked.  By the 1980s, the city knew it needed to change, seeding a hunger for reinvention that experts told me would come to define its municipally-owned internet
By the 2000s, Chattanooga had more than cleaned up its air and its reputation, building a huge aquarium in the heart of downtown and carefully revitalizing its riverfront and natural areas

But in the early aughts, with the remaining heavy industry in deep retreat, and a fragile recovery threatened by the Great Recession , the city craved a new economic engine.  The city’s EPB, which originated as a municipally owned electric utility in 1935, had already set out to build a smart electrical grid in 2008, retrofitting it with a two-way digital communications system that could detect and fix problems as they arise
This process would involve laying hundreds of miles of new fiber-optic cable lines along existing power lines, monitoring them and relaying information back and forth with operators

But as the EPB laid plans for its new grid-helping fiber, it realized that for roughly the same amount of effort and cost, it could repurpose those cables to also serve as a cutting-edge internet service.  Laying those hundreds of miles of new cables, along every single power line in the city, is an expensive and time-consuming process
But since EPB already had power lines plugging into almost every home and business throughout the city, it didn’t even need permission to get it done

And once the cables are there, there’s no real limit on how much data they can carry, meaning that they’ll work just as well whether they’re relaying the power grid’s data exclusively or if they’re carrying petabytes upon petabytes of data from hundreds of thousands of internet customers

This same quality has made it easy for EPB to pump up the volume of data it offers over the years, eventually allowing it to become the first city in the nation to offer a 25-gigabit-per-second service, which it did for its customers in 2023

More recently, EPB became the first provider nationwide to hook its fiber-optic cables up to a quantum computer — which uses advanced physics to solve mind-bogglingly complex problems — and offer its use to researchers and customers across the city.  “If we’re going to own that fiber communications network to help automate our grid, why not offer that as a service to our customers? We thought, ‘Why not go big? Why not be ambitious?’” Janet Rehberg, CEO of EPB, told me. “People thought we were crazy

And we said, ‘If we can do it, why not?’ So, we did.” Equipped with a $111 million federal stimulus grant from the recession-era American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, plus about $222 million in municipal bonds, EPB was able to complete the project — initially expected to take a decade — in just two years.  In 2010, Chattanooga became the first city in the nation to offer one-gigabit-per-second fiber optic internet.  “This was a huge shift for our city’s fortunes,” Andy Berke, mayor of Chattanooga from 2013 to 2021, told me. “All of a sudden, we were a place where you could try to discover the next big thing.”  Hundreds of startups flocked to the city for its super-fast broadband, with tech incubators setting up shop in shuttered storefronts and abandoned industrial factories dotted along the city’s downtown

In its first 10 years, EPB’s fiber network brought more than $5.3 billion in economic benefits and 10,420 jobs to the city, about 31 percent of all jobs created during that period, according to a study by the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga

This has transformed “the way we thought about ourselves and what we thought was possible technologically,” Berke said.  The broadband investment has long since paid for itself and then some in the fees people pay to access its service

EPB expects to earn about $190 million over the next year alone from its telecommunications and enormously popular internet service, all of which will flow back into the business itself or into the city
As a result, EPB chose not to increase electricity rates at all this year, in stark contrast to much of the rest of the country

And the utility now pays tens of millions of dollars annually straight back into city services, like public schools.  Under Berke’s mayoral administration, the city also integrated EPB into initiatives meant to get more Chattanoogans online

When the pandemic hit, and local schools went virtual, the city built a new program called EdConnect that saw EPB provide free internet to every family with a child who received free or reduced lunches, the first program of its kind nationwide, and one that continues to this day.  “A lot of communities set up something similar during the pandemic, but most of those are done, they kind of faded away

But we made a commitment — our community did — for 10 years, and we’re already discussing what the next 10 years looks like,” said Sammy Lowdermilk, CEO of the Enterprise Center, the nonprofit that administers EdConnect. “We’ve heard from parents using online resources to look for a job, to create resumes, to do medical research
The entire family gets to benefit from it.” Your city could have Chattanooga’s internet
Over the years, Chattanooga’s publicly owned internet has drawn countless city planners and far-flung mayors to Tennessee’s fourth-largest city to learn just how they pulled it off

But every time one visited Berke in his time in office, and every time he gave one of his “little sales pitches” on EPB’s success, over and over, they’d replied with the same refrain: “Oh, it’s incredible what you’ve done here
I mean, we can’t do it, but it’s great — good for you guys,” he recalled

Many cities don’t have a publicly owned electricity company at the ready as Chattanooga did, and many face significant barriers from state laws that restrict or heavily discourage the development of municipally owned broadband altogether.  “The number one challenge for most infrastructure projects is political

It’s the web of difficulties that make it harder to get it done.” Andy Berke, former mayor of Chattanooga Nevertheless, some places tried anyway, and many have succeeded — over 700 of them, according to Mitchell’s last count

title: Republicans are trying to make the Texas Senate race about “manliness”
excerpt: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at a campaign rally in Galveston, Texas, on October 22, 2026. | Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images Texas Attorney
body: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico speaks at a campaign rally in Galveston, Texas, on October 22, 2026. | Mark Felix/AFP via Getty Images Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton could have picked any number of messages for his first Senate campaign ad of the general election back in May
Texans care a lot about cost of living, border security, healthcare, and corruption, among other issues
But Paxton’s very first ad went with something that pollsters don’t generally ask about
He accused his opponent, Democratic state Rep
James Talarico, of being “Too Low-T for Texas. ” Too low in testosterone
Not manly enough.  Voters generally don’t rank masculinity as a top issue in any race, but Paxton’s opening salvo wasn’t completely out of left field
Young men broke for President Donald Trump by a shocking margin in 2024
During that campaign, Trump played to the “manosphere” , appearing on many a bro-y podcast and leaning on his macho, politically incorrect image for an audience burned out on the politics of Woke 1
Paxton, whom Trump endorsed over incumbent Republican Sen
John Cornyn (R-TX) in the primary, is as closely linked to the president as any candidate on the ballot — so it’s not all that surprising to see him attempt the same strategy
And Texas, after all, has its stereotypes: rugged individualism

Starting with the “Low-T” ad, the Paxton campaign has been all in on exploiting the politics of masculinity and traditional ideas about gender and gender roles to cast Talarico as not man enough to serve as senator — and the rest of the Republican ecosystem has followed suit

In May, Trump policy adviser Stephen Miller tweeted that “The Democrats made history in Texas by nominating their first transgender senate candidate.” Vice President JD Vance recently walked right up to the line of calling Talarico gay at a rally in the state
Elon Musk’s super PAC has flooded the state with AI slop commercials like this one , in which an adult drag queen in a sparkly jersey dunks on some female athletes
The commercial attacks Talarico for being supportive of trans athletes

Trump himself has also weighed in , accusing Talarico of veganism — fighting words in some Texas circles. (Talarico, 37, is a cis man, says he has a girlfriend, and denies being a vegan.) Attacks are one thing, though, and an effective political strategy another

To figure out whether Paxton’s masculinity campaign is working, the Today, Explained team headed to Texas. “People are mad about other things” At a Paxton rally in Fort Worth, Texas, on a recent Monday night, Jacenta and Susan Sims were riling each other up, seeing who could get the best dig in at Talarico’s manhood.  Susan pointed to her own chest. “My shirt says ‘No Tala-freaking-way.’ Because he is kind of a freak,” she said

She listed some of Talarico’s past comments on gender to support her statement. “Like, how are you talking about God like he’s nonbinary and there’s six sexes?”  Talarico said God was nonbinary during a Texas legislative session in 2021, making what he later described as a “cringey” point about God being above human categorization
Also in 2021, he claimed during a debate over trans kids in sports that there were six sexes
He recently walked that statement back , saying there were only two sexes
Jacenta Sims at the Paxton rally wasn’t having it: “If you really had to look deep, he’s probably got some lace on his panties
There’s nothing masculine about him.” Susan piped in, “He looks like a little boy
He’s not tough enough.” Back to Jacenta: “And we need masculinity back in Texas.” Perhaps it’s not surprising that voters who are already all in on Paxton would also be all in on this line of attack
But those are not the voters Paxton needs to convince. “I don’t care if Talarico’s gay or not
I don’t believe he is, but it wouldn’t matter to me if he is.” Jesse Sandoval said outside the Tarrant County Elections Center in Fort Worth

He’d just cast his ballot in early voting. “I just felt that they were doing that to try to deflect from the real issues.”  Another early voter, Michael, didn’t want to give his last name, and works as a cook at a local restaurant. “I just feel like this whole toxic masculinity thing is so unnecessary,” he said. “I was raised by someone who was very, very aggressive and just a very macho man

And I feel like you have to educate yourself as to why those things are not — why saying stuff like that isn’t okay, you know?” Walt Thompson, also at the polling place, said, “Because he’s soft-spoken, they feel that he’s gay
He’s just not this big rugged looking guy

They can’t accept that.” Nate, a 32-year-old construction worker who also declined to share his last name, said 2026 is a whole different moment from the last presidential election. “If this was 2024, those [messages] are effective
But I think this year it’s not gonna be effective,” he said. “People are mad about other things

When people care about gas prices, they can’t run on that.” In other words, the culture wars hit differently when you can’t afford to feed your family or drive to work.  It’s (still) the economy, stupid Matt Angle is director of the Lone Star Project, a Democratic research PAC and communications firm

He says these attacks on Talarico’s masculinity are a tell from Republicans.  “What the Republicans are worried about is people staying home,” Angle told Today, Explained . “Those people, they’re mad about the economy, they’re mad at Trump, and [Republicans] are trying to motivate them by playing to their prejudices. … They desperately need fear to be the motivator rather than anger and frustration.”  So far, it doesn’t seem to be working
Most recent polling puts Talarico in the lead
The Cook Political Report is calling the race a toss-up

The last time Texas elected a Democratic senator was 1988, but Talarico appears to have a real shot at breaking decades of Republican dominance.  Angle says Talarico’s laser focus on a message of affordability is breaking through to voters.   “They’re understanding that their salaries aren’t going as far as they should

And they like that somebody’s talking to them about the cost of groceries, the cost of housing, the cost of healthcare,” he said.  Who gets to own masculinity, anyway? There’s another key factor in how the GOP’s masculinity attacks are landing: the messenger

Paxton, after all, isn’t exactly a paragon of traditionally masculine virtue. (Just ask Trump, who can’t stop needling his hand-picked candidate for the way he dresses, looks, and talks .) According to Jill Tate, president of the Texas Federation of Republican Women, many of her members had grown skeptical of Paxton’s candidacy

Angela Paxton, filed for divorce last year on what she described as “biblical grounds.” The actual filing listed adultery as the reason for divorce.  “I’ve been involved in Texas politics over 30 years,” Tate said, “and this is the first time I’ve truly been concerned we could lose a statewide [race] since the Republicans took over in the ’90s.”  Angela Paxton recently did her ex a solid, giving a speech to the Republican women in Tate’s group called the “elephant in the room” speech

She also cut an ad boosting “the Republican ticket,” though not Paxton by name. “She talked about the fact that while our candidates may fall down and they may do things that are disappointing and morally wrong, it is extremely important to remember that that is the human side

And that’s not what they’re going to do in office,” Tate said of the speech, which urged the audience to vote for the team — for Republicans — rather than on the moral failings of one person.  Tate believes that the speech changed some minds and could push women in the room to vote for Ken Paxton instead of just staying home

title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
excerpt: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assis
body: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools
Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond
But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business
Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments

The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all
Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%)

Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here
It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business
A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms)

It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says

It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much
But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data
He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs
Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents
But the sales raise legal and ethical questions

Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups . —Matthew King Are we there yet? Interspecies communication  Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us.  Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world
A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex

Find out how close we are to interspecies communication . —Cassandra Willyard This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter
We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue

MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century
But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp
A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating
But the chief obstacle may be one of political will
